speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-ERROR IN HANSARD RESPECTING NAME OF PRESIDENT OF UGANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at page 2344 of yesterday's Hansard I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister what purpose his personal envoy, Mr. Head, has in visiting various Commonwealth countries at this time?
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave me the explanation. The passage then reads:

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-ERROR IN HANSARD RESPECTING NAME OF PRESIDENT OF UGANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what particular message was to be conveyed to General M'boto of undistinguished notoriety, the head of Uganda? What was the message to him?
The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, President M'boto is no longer president of Uganda.
As members will recall, yesterday afternoon the House was in a very happy and rather vociferous mood. I like it that way. The result was that what was said was not recorded by the reporter because it was drowned out. The Prime Minister understood me to ask about somebody I did not ask about. I asked about Amin and he thought I referred to General M'boto. He replied as I have already stated. His answer was correct, of course, because M'boto was at one time president of the Congo. Altogether, it was a comedy of errors. So that the record may be complete, I was referring and I did refer to Amin but, as I said, the House was in that feeling of high exhilaration which sometimes interferes with communication, but enjoyably so.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-ERROR IN HANSARD RESPECTING NAME OF PRESIDENT OF UGANDA
speechtext: On the same point, Mr. Speaker, there may even be more errors than the right hon. member understood because in my answer, and I did not see the blues, I did not say "President M'boto". I said "President Obote", who was indeed the president of Uganda when we had the last Commonwealth Conference, so this makes it even more complicated.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-ERROR IN HANSARD RESPECTING NAME OF PRESIDENT OF UGANDA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister for clearing up the whole matter. We all recall that even Homer nodded, so the Prime Minister and I were both in that category.

maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I will need Your Honour's advice on the validity of my question. First of
all, I would like to have the confirmation of the House that as the representative of the people in my constituency, as the representative of people who put their trust in my office, I am entitled to ask questions of the government. I should also like to have it confirmed that after I have asked these questions the answers that I get to such questions are factual and are answers on which I can base further action.
I placed on the order paper question No. 984 dealing with the Inter-American Indian Institute. It is in three parts and the questions are simple. The first part reads as follows:
Has the government been requested to join the Inter-American Indian Institute and, if so (a) by whom (b) on what date?
The third part reads as follows:
Has any employee of the government, its agencies or Crown corporations ever attended any conference meetings or symposia sponsored by the Inter-American Indian Institute over the past six years and, if so (a) who were these persons (b) on what dates-
The answers I received to these questions are less than factual. I happen to know that there was more than one attempt by the Inter-American Institute to have Canada join. There were many occasions prior to the date indicated in the answer. I also happen to know that many delegations sponsored by the Canadian government attended these meetings.
These facts, Mr. Speaker, are underlined by a secret or confidential document which obviously is no longer confidential because I received it this morning. In it, an official of the government indicates that the answer to question No. 1 is less than factual. Another section outlines the reasons why the government is embarrassed about the Inter-American Indian institute. I quote from the document:
Indian leaders might be tempted on occasion to use the International Indian Institute as a forum in which they could put forward their grievances against the federal government.
Another paragraph in the document reads as follows:
The composition of the International Institute would need to be carefully conceived as it could generate friction among native people in that it would be undesirable and, in any event, virtually impossible to exclude representation from the Metis and nonstatus Indian groups.
These are the reasons the answers to my questions are not correct. Here is yet another cabinet leak. As a result, I should like to move the following motion, if I may do so, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Taylor):
That this matter dealing with the International Indian Institute be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections or to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext:
Hon. members do from time to time bring to the attention of the House and the Chair the complaints
2384

March 20, 1973
Privilege
or grievances as to the contents of answers given to their questions. It is a long established rule that these grievances, although they may be the subject of a debate, cannot found a question of privilege. I refer the hon. member to citation 113 of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition:
Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in debates or in the proceedings of the House. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament.
And further:
A dispute arising between two members as to allegations of facts does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
The hon. member suggests that information conveyed to him in reply to a question on the order paper is incorrect. That may be so. The hon. member said that he was seeking my advice. My advice to him and to the House, and my ruling at the same time, is that I cannot find there is a prima facie question of privilege here which should be put to the House for debate at this time.

maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the hon. member told us he has a document which he described as "another cabinet leak", and as he quoted from this document, I wonder whether he would be prepared to table it so that it could be before the House in the proper manner. I realize this is a somewhat delicate matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: The rules do not, of course, provide for the tabling of documents, even official documents or so-called confidential documents, quoted in the House by private members. The rule only applies when such a document is quoted in debate by members of the government. It cannot apply to hon. members generally. The suggestion is very often made in debate, when hon. members refer to or quote from a document, that the document in question be tabled. Certainly we would become involved in a very complicated practice, a practice which could easily lead to abuse, if we made it possible for members generally to table documents. I think that is not the purpose of the rule deeding with the tabling of documents.

maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: In the light of your ruling, Mr. Speaker-and I must agree with Your Honour that the rule does not apply in this case, which is why I suggested this was a somewhat delicate matter-perhaps the House would give unanimous consent to the document being tabled in the circumstances, bearing in mind the allegation the hon. member has made and that it seems to be a genuine document.

maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: Obviously there is not unanimous agreement. In any case I would hesitate to seek the unanimous consent of the House to allow a private member to table a document. I doubt whether this would be a good practice in which to become involved.

maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: May I make one more comment?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: The hon. member should resume his seat. He can, perhaps, rise on a point of order but there should certainly be no debate after a ruling has been made. I will hear the hon. member if he has a point of order.

maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: The point concerns your reference to my conflict with another member of the House. It is not with another member of the House. It is with the Department of Indian Affairs and the government as a whole.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. OBERLE-ANSWER TO ORDER PAPER QUESTION NO.
speechtext: The hon. member is, of course, doing what I suggested he cannot do once a ruling has been made.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
That this House, noting that the government has failed to bring about an integrated overall national transportation policy, and further noting the inadequacies of ministerial response to Canada's transportation problems, deplores the government's failure to recognize that Canada's transportation is vital to Canadian unity, regional equality, the encouragement of resource development, the increase of international and domestic trade and the betterment of the urban and rural quality of life and urges that immediate action be taken to establish an over-all national transportation policy to bring about these obiectives.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I present this motion to the House this afternoon on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party. I believe the motion bears particular significance inasmuch as the minister responsible for transport has said very little about transportation during the present parliament. I believe, also, it is obvious that the government has failed to recognize the fact that there is, indeed, a transportation problem in this country and that it must be tackled immediately.

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
I am sure there is no one here who doubts that one of the most important issues facing Canada today is the need to develop a sound, co-ordinated, futuristic transportation system. Indeed, it is fair to say that developments in the next 20 years will play a major part in defining that future. On September 1, 1966, when the Hon. J. W. Pick-ersgill introduced his new policy for transportation, he spoke in glowing terms of what it would mean for the future. According to Mr. Pickersgill, a framework had been created in which transportation would operate not only to serve the public but also to better insure the Canadian treasury and the Canadian taxpayer against unnecessary and undue charges, and, in some cases, duplicated charges for duplicated services. Unfortunately, the government has totally failed to develop a national transportation policy-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
-pursuant to section 3 of the National Transportation Act, and has failed to take measures to revitalize and rebuild Canadian transportation so as to meet present and future needs. As a result of this inaction, we have failed to achieve the two goals of which Mr. Pickersgill spoke. The public is not getting the kind of service to which he referred, nor are taxpayers relieved of what he described as unnecessary and undue charges levied against them.
As a result of the legislation brought down in 1966, the railways have parliament and the minister right where they want them. The companies eliminate services, remove railway stations, close crossings, raise freight rates without any regard for the effects on the people concerned, without any regard for social disruption or the impact on the economy, particularly on the economy of the smaller communities affected. Yet, the people pay. They pay the price in huge subsidies and they pay the price by being deprived of services.
I believe the railways have an obligation not only to provide services. I believe they also have a social and moral responsibility. They grew as this nation grew. They form an integral part of our country. Though now through government hand-outs and their own approach to business they have become stale and stagnant. They have adopted a policy of driving business away, especially in the area of passenger traffic. There is plenty of evidence to support this contention. I am sure every member of the House has received communications from throughout the country critical of railway passenger service. While this is going on, losses climb and taxpayers foot the bill. At the same time, they must suffer discontinuation of services, loss of facilities, confusion and frustration.
One wonders what to expect from the government. The Speech from the Throne contained some reference to transportation but used words like "explore", "examine", and "recognize". Such words can only lead one to conclude that the government is without a policy to deal with transportation issues, though this area is vital to the future of our social and economic fabric. I think it is time we took a bold, new approach toward solving the transportation problems of this country. It is imperative that we do so. The government's inaction is a further manife-

station of its bankruptcy of ideas and its total failure to communicate with the provinces and with the people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I repeat that bold, positive initiatives must be taken. In the Speech from the Throne the government, as its fourth economic objective, proposed to ensure "that all regions benefit from the prosperity brought about by an expanding economy". No one can argue with that objective. The objective, however commendable, cannot, and I submit will not, be achieved without overcoming some of the gross inequities that are prevalent in our transportation system, particularly as they affect the western provinces and the maritime regions in our country. I say to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that if he wants to stamp out western alienation let him start with an equitable transportation system and an equitable freight rate structure. No longer is the west interested in simply supplying raw materials and export jobs to the central regions of Canada. If the minister wants the economy of the Atlantic provinces to flourish, let him overhaul the transportation system. For far too long now inept transportation policies have stymied growth and development in this region.
It was just last week that two of our national farm organizations met with Members of Parliament and with the government in the city of Ottawa. Both of these farm organizations used words like "urgent", "critical" and "crucial" with reference to the challenge of overcoming the problems in our transportation system. They advised us that it is vital to overcome some of the inequitable features of our transportation policy if the needs of our agricultural industry are to be met, particularly in the area of fruits and vegetables. If this country is to maintain its leadership role in the supplying of nutritious foods at reasonable cost, it is vital that we take positive steps to overcome transportation inequities as they relate to the maritime provinces. Furthermore, if we are to develop to a greater degree the processing of our agricultural products in the areas where they are produced, then it is imperative too that we institute a more equitable transportation scheme.
What is the government doing about this, Mr. Speaker? In particular, what is the minister doing about this problem? The minister says that he is enjoying his post, but are we getting any leadership from the government or from this minister?

The answer, of course, is no. What I say is in no way to be construed as a personal attack upon the minister; I know him to be a very personable and amiable chap. He may even be somewhat sympathetic to the needs of transportation. But I am not really sure whether he is interested in transportation, and I am not so sure that he is really happy about his portfolio. Above all,
I am not sure that he is really serious about the importance of his portfolio. Perhaps he might enlighten us a little today.
When we review the performance of this minister in this parliament during the period January 4, 1973 to March 12, 1973 the minister is found to have replied inadequately to about 108 questions in this House of Commons. The minister's answers to questions that have been directed to him are punctuated with expressions such as "I think"; "I do not think"; "I believe"; "I do not know"; "I will inquire"; "I will take notice"; "I cannot"; "I am not aware"; "It may be"; "it might"; "it probably"; "I will check"; "when"; "it is very difficult", "in a few weeks"; "as soon as" and "I hope".

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I am very happy to see the minister checking some of these punctuated expressions, and as I said before this should certainly not be construed as a personal attack upon the minister. I appreciate the fact that he is taking it in good form.
Furthermore, the minister seems to engage in a game of buck-passing, perhaps because of his lack of knowledge, or because of his attitude toward hon. members on this side of the House, or because of the government's lack of policy. I must say that his repertoire of non-commital catch-phrases serves him exceptionally well in warding off any commitments by his department or the government. This non-commital, non-answer philosophy of the minister can only result in further confusion and disservice to Canadians in an area where an effective policy is most essential in combatting regional disparity and promoting national unity.
When the minister spoke in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, he even failed to mention transportation or to elaborate to any degree on the promises which were put forward in the Speech from the Throne. Instead, he harped about the French-English language problem with reference to the election backlash. When he was asked in the House whether he would tell the House what he intends to do about our transportation problems, he simply ignored the question. He engaged in a game of chastising some hon. members for raising certain issues during the election campaign.
In addition, the minister has repeatedly promised in this House to look into such matters as rail line abandonment, rail passenger service, improved airline service, station agency closures, price competition among our airlines. We have not received any answers to these questions. Most of the answers that he has given us are in the form I have just described He and other ministers preceding him have often shrugged off inquiries about increasing travel and freight costs by stating that the Canadian Transport Commission has the authority over such matters. The Canadian Transport Commission itself is an ineffective, misguid-
Transportation Policy
ed and confused authoritative body under the semi-leadership of the Minister of Transport and the direct guidance of Mr. Benson. The latest example is the fiasco of the manner in which it handled the ABC charter regulations, which from time of inception created confusion, and even today we still do not know what is the accurate interpretation of these charter regulations.
The CTC has not carried out the duties assigned to it by Section 3 of the National Transportation Act. It has not concerned itself with the needs of the public and those who use the services of our transportation system; rather it has dedicated itself to the protection and preservation of our airlines and the railways.
Part III of the National Transportation Act which deals with motor vehicle transport is no closer to being implemented today than it was when the act was written, notwithstanding the fact that there have been a number of federal-provincial consultations in this regard. This is most discouraging, Mr. Speaker, and it is unfair to the trucking industry because of the lack of uniformity in highway regulations from province to province. Failure to implement Part III of the act makes it virtually impossible for the Canadian Transport Commission to respond effectively to Section 21 of the act, the object of which is to co-ordinate and harmonize the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by rail, water, aircraft, motor vehicle and pipeline. Truckers, particularly those from western Canada, tell us that it is easier for them to travel the American routes than the trans-Canada route because of the different regulations from province to province. Does that promote national unity Mr. Speaker? Definitely not!
The present minister and his predecessors have persistently said that they have no authority over the Canadian Transport Commission. Whether this is merely passing the buck or a reluctance on their part to become involved in aiding Canadians in the midst of the transportation crisis, I am not sure. However, it appears, according to the ministers, that the Canadian Transport Commission is an autonomous entity and parliament cannot control it. If this is the case, I suggest that the structure should be revamped so that its decisions will not continue to have the detrimental effects they now produce not only on Canadians but on the economy as well.
I want to say to the minister, through you Mr. Speaker, that the answers we have been getting to the transportation problems that effect our country are far from satisfactory. I believe it is fair to say that hon. members on this side of the House are not going to tolerate these nonanswers for much longer. I do not believe we are going to tolerate the inexcusable lack of action in various areas of the transportation portfolio. I believe that the time has come when the minister should start levelling with us in the House of Commons and give us some of the information that we so rightly deserve.
However, I am informed that there may be a new era coming. I am informed that a gentleman by the name of Jim Davey has been assigned to the office of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). According to my information he was previously attached to the Prime Minister's office and was in charge of special projects.

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy

speechtext:
Mr. Davey has an interesting background as evidenced by his two most recent occupations. He was formerly the vice president of the chartered accountant firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. of Toronto, the firm which was involved in the controversial CNR auditor switch. This was the move that saw the auditor changed via the Benson-Turner formula without parliamentary approval. After this, he was employed as a systems coordinator for Canadian National Railways. His recent assignment to the office of the Minister of Transport may be of significance, since he is considered somewhat of an expert in the transportation field. I am sure that all hon. members on this side of the House will be looking forward to his performance with great interest.
Now, I should like to refer briefly to the matter of freight rates and the discriminatory effect of their structure in the country. That this is so was agreed by many prominent members of the other place when an interesting debate took place there. There is no doubt that freight rates are not only retarding growth in western Canada but are aiding the increased feeling of western alienation toward the rest of Canada. If the Minister of Transport is so concerned about national unity, as was evident in the Speech from the Throne debate, why has he failed to introduce constructive measures to promote this cause in the field of transportation? Shortly after the election the former minister of transport said in Alberta that Alberta must get more industry. According to local newspaper reports, he admitted that Ottawa is to blame for the condition of the economy in the west, and said that a lot of the trouble was due to the fact that we do not have an effective, over-all transportation policy. But what did he do about it? Nothing!

speechtext: They moved him out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
He realized, after the election, that there was a problem. Western Canada is deeply concerned about discriminatory freight rates, rail line abandonment, station closings, and the reduction of passenger service. It is also concerned about the rationalization taking place in the transportation and handling facilities with respect to grain. We do not know what the government's policy is in this area, but if it does not have a policy perhaps it should delay withdrawing services and closing stations until an adequate and effective review of the situation has been undertaken.
In the Maritimes, the Council of Maritime Premiers has recently condemned the policies of Canada's two major railways. The reasoning behind this is a charge that the railways and the federal government fail to understand the transportation problems of the Atlantic provinces. Most maritime businessmen say that high freight rates and federal transportation policies retard industrial development in the region. The situation has become serious enough to induce the three provinces to embark on a joint effort to tackle regional transportation problems.
Obviously, if this is the case, the federal government's ability to combat the regional disparities in its so-called transportation policy is sadly lacking. If the provinces must take the initiative, then what useful purpose does the

federal department and the Canadian Transport Commission serve? The same thing is going on in western Canada where the ministers of the three prairie provinces have met to discuss economic objectives, the question of transportation as an instrument of economic policy, railway abandonment and railway structure. The initiative comes from them, Mr. Speaker and not from this minister. Why? This government's approach to federal transportation matters is not good enough. The federal government must develop a policy to co-ordinate all transportation systems or the economic growth of all Canadian regions will suffer. The failure to do so will give rise to further dissatisfaction in the realm of federal-provincial relations, and will create a great deal more alienation and ill-feeling because of regional disparities.
This government has only paid lip service to the demand of the provinces with regard to transportation. Transportation built this country, Mr. Speaker, when the Canadian Pacific Railway linked east and west, and now this link has fallen apart leaving in its wake regional disparities and dissension. There is a lack of planning, a lack of initiative and in view of the inflationary pressures involved, it is urgent that this situation be corrected. As transportation costs increase, so does the price of the goods which must use the transportation systems. The government's inadequacy in this area is severely restricting the economy of the regions. If we were to delve more deeply into the problem, I am sure that we would find one of the root causes to be the failure of the Canadian Transport Commission.
The hold-down policy of the government is interwoven with evidence of a lack of social consciousness of the decisions handed down by the CTC. If the ministry of transport cannot come up with a formula to combat the mismanagement of transportation-and we have some doubt about this because this administration is pretty shaky-then I suggest we should recommend that the Canadian Transport Commission answer to a special parliamentary committee and ensure us that this violation of the public interest will be stopped. If the government and the Minister of Transport cannot come up with an effective transportation policy, then I believe it is time that we had some answers because there is ample evidence outlining the problems. There has been study upon study, and there is no shortage of evidence. I would recommend that a parliamentary committee be struck which would be empowered to study and review this whole matter.
As I say, a great deal of urgency must be attached to this particular question. The government must show a willingness to grapple with the problem and, above all, must show a willingness to accept in a serious way some of the recommendations which may emanate from such a committee study. In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I simply say we are looking for leadership from this government in the area of transportation, and if it cannot supply that leadership we shall.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party welcome the presentation of this motion by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). In fact, I am even a
March 20,1973

little jealous. I wish we had got there first. However we welcome it. Until some significant changes are made in and about transportation in Canada, it is a matter which should come before this parliament as often as possible. In a country like Canada all aspects of transportation must be treated as essential public services, public services at cost. A national policy and legislation must be designed to effect that objective. I submit that transportation is in the same category so far as Canadian public need is concerned as streets, highways, sewers, water systems, post offices, electric power and telephones. Transportation is an essential public utility. A major revision, and in some ways a reversal, is required in respect of the National Transportation Act. What is required is a major revision of the principles underlying the present archaic approach to transportation which has its roots in the national policy of the 19th century.
In the 1870's, the much subsidized CPR was seen as a vehicle for achieving an integrated national economy from the Atlantic to the Pacific and for joining this country of Canada from sea to sea. In contrast, the National Transportation Act of 1967 states that the national interest is best served by developing an economic, efficient and adequate transportation system, making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest possible cost. With this kind of transportation act, the federal government's foresight, and the foresight of the Canadian Transport Commission, is now restricted to economic efficiency within the transportation system itself. The monopolistic providers of the service can therefore proceed toward their own internal development, and their own objectives, unencumbered by and without regard for any broad national economic or social considerations. This is, in fact, the essence of the hinterland exploitation mentality as it exists today in respect of the whole question of transportation.
The most glaring example of this is the discriminatory setting of freight rates on everything but grain. The railway companies are legally free to maximize revenues where they can. Prairie customers, and to some extent the Maritimes as well, are captives of the railways because of the nature of the goods they have to ship and receive and the length of haul. The west is subject to horizontal freight rate increases and an inequitable transcontinental rate structure. This is an intolerable situation in relation to the development of secondary industry in the west. I should like to give some examples to remind this House again and remind the people of central Canada what is and has been developing in respect of freight rates.
Let us take angles, beams and other steel products. From Contrecoeur, Quebec to Vancouver, the revenue per ton mile is $1.02 while to Regina it is $2.55. In this case, the revenue is more than double. The distance from Contrecoeur to Regina is 1,200 miles less than the distance to Vancouver. The situation with respect of Saskatoon is even worse. The revenue per ton mile is $2.59 compared to $1.02 to Vancouver.
Let us take wire, nails, staples, wire fencing and other steel products. From Sydney, Nova Scotia to Vancouver the revenue per ton mile is 95 cents. To Regina it is $1.77. To Saskatoon it is $1.88. Then, let us take some foodstuffs. I might say that these rates are all taken from the tariffs
Transportation Policy
of the railways which are available to the public. On a
100,000	pound carload the revenue per ton mile from any point in Ontario to Vancouver is $1.41. To Regina it is $2.63, and to Saskatoon $2.73. The tariff on foodstuffs from points in Quebec to Vancouver is $1.35 per ton mile. To Regina it is $2.36 and to Saskatoon it is $2.46.	[DOT]

speechtext: May I say to the right hon. gentleman that the situation in respect of Prince Albert, North Bat-tleford or Swift Current is even worse. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
My colleague asks why. It is because of the Canadian geographical situation. Many Canadians are penalized because they happen to live in the far north, in the Maritimes or on the Prairies. I fail to understand why a system of equalized and/or subsidized freight rates cannot be applied all over Canada. The cost of transportation forms a large part of the cost of living in Canada. For example, as I mentioned in the budget debate, Canadian citizens living in Fond du Lac, Saskatchewan have to pay 95 cents a quart for milk. Almost two-thirds of that price is transportation cost.
Because our transportation act of 1967 allows our railways to do what is best for them, the best interests of Canada and Canadians are not being served. Besides discriminatory freight rates of 100 years standing, there has been and is now a continuing downgrading and erosion of railway services in this country. There is a reduced or non-existent passenger service. Secondary and branch rail lines have been allowed to deteriorate to the point of being a disgrace. Rail line abandonments have been announced by the companies which will result in the death of dozens of communities which could and should otherwise be viable. There is an outrageous lack of effort and funds for research and development of modern, faster and safer rail transportation components, particularly in respect of trains and tracks.
I find it passing strange that a national government can allocate $67 million in research and development to private aircraft manufacturers for a short take-off and landing aircraft to haul 15 or 20 people, yet have a dearth of funds in respect of research and development for rail transport or other forms of ground transportation. Canadian National, practically single handed, is carrying on research and development into the turbo train. It gets all the brickbats and this government sits as a patsy for private aircraft manufacturers, most of whom are American owned. Several successive federal governments have been party to and have encouraged the de-emphasizing of rail transportation with a disproportionate priority given to the airlines, most of which are privately owned.

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
The CNR, as a publicly-owned rail system, is only paid lip service by the government. It is required to operate under financial handicaps and outmoded economic standards that effectively prevent it from adequately serving' the Canadian people and the nation. Successive national governments have set up public utilities, such as the CNR and Air Canada, and then have handicapped them with debt structure or limited operational ability to the aid and comfort of the privately owned sectors of transportation. I want to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker, particularly for the benefit of my good friend the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). Successive old line party governments do not want, in fact do not dare to have, public utilities such as CNR and Air Canada succeed, as they can and should succeed.
Outmoded theories of competition between our national transportation systems effectively prevent the development of rail and air services to Canadians in all parts of Canada on an equitable basis. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians are discriminated against or ignored in the provision of transportation service which, I repeat, surely is an essential public service and a public utility. The concept of profitability as the main criterion for national transportation systems, inevitably, and by the very nature of transportation, results in inadequate, inefficient and unfair treatment of Canadian transportation needs.
Now, I would like to move to air transportation. Our publicly owned national air transportation system began in 1937. Trans-Canada Air Lines, with the backing of the federal government and of the people of Canada, were given the task of building, operating and gradually extending a national air transport system to serve Canada coast to coast. At a time when the great private, free enterprises could not and would not do it, the people of Canada, through their own public utility, took on the task of establishing a national air transportation system. Again, successive national governments gave lip service to our own publicly-owned system.
As Trans-Canada Air Lines and then Air Canada grew and succeeded, as its prospects, even for profitability and certainly for growth, appeared most attractive, the erosion of their position as a national and international air carrier began. Both old line parties, as governments, followed policies to make available to private enterprise, mostly the CPR, franchises and routes that should have gone to the system that the people of Canada built and own. But no, the CPR was to be again provided for at the expense of our Crown corporation as well as the Canadian public; it was given the gravy. For a number of years we have had an air transportation policy. It is not Orwellian, it is Pickersgillian. That policy is based on a theory which is still held by both the old line parties. The theory is that Air Canada should serve Europe and the Caribbean area, while the CPR should serve the Pacific and Central and South America. What happened?
The next thing we knew the Pickersgillian policy was ignored and CP Air was granted routes to Amsterdam, Lisbon and Madrid. My grade 5 or 6 geography tells me that those cities are in Europe and that particularly Amsterdam is in northern Europe. But CP Air got those routes and all the while our own airline, Air Canada,

continued to be excluded from the Pacific countries. Even if one were to live up to this asinine Pickersgillian policy, it is surely not logical, on the one hand, to allow CP Air to intrude into routes into Europe and, on the other, to exclude Air Canada from the Pacific countries. Surely, that situation should not be allowed to continue. In spite of an Air Canada application, CP Air was awarded the routes to Shanghai and Peking. Even while it grows, the government keeps Air Canada on the borderline of success. That whole policy needs to be radically changed, if not completely thrown out.
Similarly, on domestic routes, private regional carriers continue to be granted fat routes that Air Canada developed and that are supported by the Canadian public. The government continues to grant fat routes to private carriers which further prevents Air Canada from prospering as much as it should and prevents it from providing better services on new, isolated routes or on the less lucrative routes I suppose the classic case of the old line party pork barrel when it comes to airline routes is the granting of a route to Transair from Winnipeg to Thunder Bay to Sault Ste. Marie to Toronto, a route which is in the top ten of the best routes of Air Canada. It is passing strange. Prior to Transair being granted that route they had options on the purchase of two big four motor jets. It is passing strange that an executive assistant of one Jack Pickersgill was on the board of directors of Transair. It is passing strange that the Liberal candidate in the Selkirk by-election, within a matter of weeks after the by-election, became an executive assistant to the president of Transair. As I say, Transair got one of the ten best routes of Air Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Collusion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: That is not honest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Air Canada has been placed in such a position that, in another 20 or 30 years, it will be like CNR; it will have a debt load that it can never repay and it will never be allowed to truly function as a national and international carrier representing Canada. The best it will be able to do will be to continue to be eroded and to be ignored in favour of outfits like CPR.
May I say a word about some other areas of transportation. Pipelines are surely public utilities as are other kinds of transportation service. A pipeline is an essential public service and should be publicly owned. It is a common carrier and part and parcel of our entire transportation system. Private enterprise has no relevance, is too inefficient and too costly, to control parts of our national and international transportation systems.
In the area of harbours I would like to ask my good friend, the hon. member for Vegreville, if he really believes that the financial and political powers in his party in central Canada will allow any downgrading or lessening of the importance of ports such as Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto in order to make sure that the port of Churchill is really developed, as well as ports such as Prince Rupert and other ports similar to those two. No way, Mr. Speaker. I have heard a great deal of support expressed by prairie Conservative members for the development of the Port of Churchill. Mr. Speaker, for six years they had an opportunity to do something really
March 20, 1973

imaginative about Churchill and Prince Rupert, and they blew it. The capacity of the Port of Churchill can be doubled and tripled within the next two years. Icebreaking services need to be improved. Wharf facilities, terminal facilities, and other ancillary services required at the port need to be constructed. A sum of $100 million or $200 million needs to be injected into the port, and a further $100 million should be spent on upgrading rail line service into the port. But this government, like all the other old line governments, has the imagination of a doorknob. If something is going to detract from Vancouver, Montreal or Toronto, then it will not do it. That is the government's way. And then members of the government wonder about alienation, and disaffection with it throughout great regions of the country.
I want to submit to the House, Mr. Speaker, what the NDP believes in and supports as part of a national transportation policy. The first and central thrust of such a policy should be that interprovincial and national transportation systems are an essential public services, and should be treated as public utilities which will provide service at cost, with profitability taking second place. An NDP government would bring about public ownership of the CP system, not just of its railway but of its airlines, its ships, pipelines, mineral rights, and various processing plants which it now operates. Everything that the Canadian Pacific system has built up over the years has been derived from the grants of money and land made to it, with the consequent siphoning-off of railway profits into other operations such as high rise office buildings and land speculation. What business the CPR ever had in getting into such things is something I do not know.
An NDP government would bring about a transfer of the balance of the CNR public debt-almost $2 billion-to the government of Canada in exchange for an equivalent value of shares, thus making the people of Canada the sole owners of our railway system. An NDP government would also bring about public ownership of interprovincial and multiprovincial pipelines. We would bring about a combination of equalized and/or subsidized passenger, freight, express and telecommunication rates right across Canada, in order to eliminate discrimination against Canadian citizens and enterprises because of geographical location, and apply such rates to the kinds of goods that people in all areas need to ship and receive.
Immediately needed is a five-year moratorium on railway branch line abandonment and agency closures, and we should halt and reverse the over centralization of customer service centres. Mr. Speaker, I see you are about to get to your feet, and I would like to tell you that I should be able to finish in about two minutes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate your kindness and that of my colleagues. I shall conclude quickly.
The seventh thing the NDP believes in and would bring about as a government would be the complete integration of rail, air and ground transportation services. Surely, it is nonsensical to waste so much money and investment on trying to improve air service from downtown Ottawa to downtown Montreal, considering that those two cities are so close together. I suspect that even now one can get as quickly by bus or rail from Ottawa to Montreal as one can get by air from downtown Ottawa to downtown Montreal. Surely, the current expenditure on this air service is a waste. Our ground and rail transportation systems suffer as a result. All three modes of transportation should be integrated, particularly rail and bus service for certain short hauls, and rail and air service for long hauls. The equalization of air fares is also essential for the movement of people in Canada. Without equalized air fares, people who live in Inuvik or Yellowknife are discriminated against outrageously simply because they do not happen to live in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto.
The eighth thing an NDP government would do would be to undertake massive public investment into research, development and production of turbo, air cushion and monorail transportation for intercity and city transportation systems. Our metropolitan areas alone cannot cope with the necessary research and development, let alone with the installation and operation of the new kinds of systems that are required.
I close by saying that we must quit handicapping the public transportation utilities, mainly Air Canada and Canadian National Railways. We must quit preventing them from being the kind of success that they can and should be. We must quit stacking the decks against public enterprises in transportation systems. We must quit doing such ridiculous things as having Air Canada go to the New York financial market to issue $26,633,000 worth of securities, none of which were offered for sale to the Canadian public, all of which were offered for sale in the United States, half of which were bought by four U.S. insurance companies and bonding companies, with the rest going to what are called institutional investors in the United States. This is shameful. It should make any Minister of Transport blush. And all of this money went for the leasing of 2 Lockheed aircraft after the government let $50 million go down the drain on a Canadian hydrofoil. Surely the people of Canada would have provided that kind of investment money for Air Canada.
The transportation systems of Canada must become public utilities. They must be publicly owned. The sole basis of their operations must be service to Canadians, moving goods and people at cost, without discrimination against where people live. This means equalization of fares, freight and express costs. Without these things this country cannot stay as united as it should be. Without these, sections of our country will still feel angry and alienated. But with these things we can have the kind of transportation system of which we are capable, a system that can operate in a northern climate over vast distances, and that can serve citizens in any part, and I stress any part, of the Dominion of Canada.

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very happy to participate in the debate on the motion presented by the Progressive Conservative party and which reads as follows:
That this House, noting that the government has failed to bring about an integrated overall National Transportation Policy, and further noting the inadequacies of ministerial response to Canada's transportation problems, deplores the Government's failure to recognize that Canada's transportation is vital to Canadian unity, regional equality, the encouragement of resource development, the increase of international and domestic trade and the betterment of the urban and rural quality of life-urges that immediate action be taken to establish an overall National Transportation Policy to bring about these objectives.
Mr. Speaker I am very happy to see that the minister is here. I think he is noting our remarks and I hope that this day will be more fruitful than all the speeches we have been making for years.
I recall the period of Mr. Donald Gordon, the years of struggle. We have known difficult years which bore more fruit than all the years we are living now.
At that time at least, the president of the Canadian National reacted but for some years, we seem to be running our head against a wall: the more we talk, the less effect it has. I think that if things keep going as they are now, in my area at least, the Canadian National will disappear.
Today I want to talk a little about the CN and then deal with our air service.
Are we justified in comparing what it costs the country to administer a company like the Canadian National, in return for the services provided? I think any hon. member is shocked when he is made aware of the disbursements of the Canadian National. For example, a bill in favour of the Canadian National that has just been introduced in the House, sets forth the estimated requirements of this company for 1973.
The Canadian National, in spite of all its receipts, says that in 1973 it will have to invest $138,978,000 in railway properties, $13 million I in branch lines, $31,897,000 in equipment, $25,946,000 in telecommunications, $5,679,000 in hotels and $8,800,000 in the CN Tower Limited, for a grand total of $225.5. And we are told what to expect for 1974, costs of $75 million and a few $100 million, with an almost unlimited borrowing power.
I wonder when the government will finally realize that perhaps the civil servants do not play their part in an impeccable manner. I do not blame the minister because he just assumed his new responsibilities. I am sure he is not more responsible of that situation than I could be myself, but the CN high ranking officials have full powers and they are those who are responsible for the astronomical administration cost of the services provided by the company.
Quite a few things can be seen in this administration, Mr. Speaker. Really, it is to be wondered whether the administrators want to give more services to the Canadians or if they simply want to break the government of Canada through the CN. The more we go-and they call

this evolution-the more the offices are filled with personnel, the more we see people getting annual salaries of $30,000, $35,000, $50,000 or $60,000. What are they doing in those offices? I ask you.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: They are not doing much.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
As the hon. member said, they are not doing much.
So as to increase this personnel they are reducing the number of men assigned to various services so that now they are getting involved in the construction of hotels.
Some civil servants are convinced that the CN is a hotel system whereas it is a transportation service. They forget that the people needed to fill up these hotels must get there by railways. I warn my dear civil servant friends that if they want their luxury hotels to turn a profit they must first send back a fair number of workmen on the railway to fix it and to make it more accessible to "big transportation" because we have had more derailments over the last few years than ever before.
Let us consider the losses caused these last few years by derailments. There are no more maintenance crews. We now have three foremen for one every maintenance man. I think the government will have to get involved and remove some freedom from all these senior officials who only dream of grandeur.
In my constituency, a servo-centre was established. Mr. Speaker, that is a wonderful thing. I even went to the opening of that centre, about which the following was said and I quote:
The establishment of this centre is a significant step in the CN service improvement program. That program provides for the establishment of a country wide servo-centre network, under which one of the most modern data processing systems will be made available to customers in the most distant areas.
I wonder where the Canadian National gets its customers in our area because the only people using the CN are the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, Domtar Chemical Limited and four or five big manufacturers. It seems as though everything had been built for their benefit.
However, we read this:
The establishment of these centres in Canada concerns two essential railroad services: full carloads and express transport.
At the end, they say:
Servo-centres will also include passenger services and telecommunications.
Once more I wish to draw the attention of the House on passenger services. I said a while ago that the more progress we made the less service we got. We had two sleeping-cars last year, but today there is only one third of one. As a matter of fact, there are a few berths at the end of the lounge car and they call that the sleeping-car for the whole of the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area. Quite an achievement considering all the money the CN is getting in our area. Let us not forget that in Quebec it is from our area that the CN gets most of its freight transport revenue. And I had figures published in this regard.
March 20, 1973

Not only is there no sleeping car but the coaches are not even clean, which is not likely to attract customers, so that each year their number decreases. When one has travelled by train once, one thinks twice before doing it again.
During my last trip, it took me exactly 20 hours to cover 400 miles. I spent 20 hours on the train-practically a work week-and the 40-hour week on the train is much more difficult than my 40, 60 or 70-hour work week.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: It is less of a strain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Because it is less shaky.
Once more, I simply wanted to draw the attention of the House to this, because I have also heard that, for many years, senior officials have been willing to eliminate the passenger service, at least between Chambord and Dol-beau, or between Chambord and Chicoutimi.
As far as the servo-centre is concerned, I do not know who carried out the study, but we know that Chambord is the centre of the region since connections for the whole region of the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean are made there. And in Chambord, there is nothing left! A servo-centre was established at the other end of the line, in Jonquiere, and another in Saint-Felicien, while had there been only one service in Chambord, the whole region could have been covered. But no, it was deemed useful to spend money and establish two servo-centres. Consequently, the service is quite unsatisfactory.
Before, in Chambord, they used to repair coaches or locomotives. Everything was closed down. When a car or a locomotive breaks down it is hooked onto the back of the train and brought back to Montreal for repair. A valve cannot even be repaired in Chambord. I have even seen passenger cars frozen stiff during winter. They have to be brought back to Montreal for defreezing whereas before mechanics used to repair them on the spot. All that was done away with to modernize and centralize. It is because of problems like that that we no longer have passenger services.
I do not want to take all my time to talk about the Canadian National because I have talked about it on several occasions here and because I am convinced that the result of this debate today will amount to a big zero. But I think that if people decided-

speechtext:
No. I have no confidence left. I hope the minister will try and restore confidence. As a matter of fact, he does all he can to restore confidence during election time. He promises the moon and stars but you do not see him afterwards. I like it when he comes to my riding, not when he comes just to make promises but to launch projects.
I hope that this time the minister will listen to us.
Turning to another subject I would like now to say a few words about Roberval airport. It is again an issue that
Transportation Policy
this minister knows very well because he actually walked on the runway at Roberval. He will remember that in the month of June 1972 the city of Roberval sent him a resolution from the minutes of the meeting of the city of Roberval which read as follows:
The Mayor told the members of the Council about the meeting with Messrs. Beaudry, Coulombe and Taillon of the Department of Transport. The latter announced that major alterations would be carried out at the municipal airport. Only 3,500 feet of the airstrip will be used, closing off a very bumpy section, while still allowing the safe landing of some types of aircrafts.
When a runway is damaged, instead of having it repaired, only part of it is used. Very soon, it will just be long enough for toy airplanes. Let me quote further:
The landing beacons will be set up accordingly and the existing ones will remain unused along the closed-off section. The 3,500-foot airstrip will be marked with white-painted lines as on the model provided and the costs will be incurred by the city.
The government could not even afford to get the white lines painted: he had the city pay for them. I continue with the question:
Following this statement, the following resolution was passed: It is moved by councillor Philippe-Auguste Morin, seconded by councillor Leonce Desgagne and unanimously resolved that the council of the City of Roberval make the Department of Transport aware of its disapproval concerning this decision and that it urges the said department to proceed immediately with the repair of the runway so as to make it usable on its whole length. Where minor repairs were involved, the City of Roberval assumed responsibility for them in accordance, as much as possible, with its contract with the Department. In the same contract, it is provided that any major repair is the sole responsibility of the department. It goes without saying that this work should be done at the Department's expense, even though the cost of the repairs are of a sizeable amount. The City of Roberval having invested over $600,000 in the development of the airport, the Department should realize the great extent of its participating and provide immediately for repairs.
Well, many representations have been made, in particular on June 28, 1972 when they acknowledged receipt of a letter I had written to the present minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) who was then Minister of Transport. I will quote another letter that I received from the city of Roberval. It stated:
To follow up our telephone call, please find herewith a copy of a letter we received from Mr. Baribeau, regional director of Quebec,...
And Mr. Baribeau's letter reads as follows:
Thank you for your letter of December 20, 1971 regarding the runway of your municipal airport which seems to have caused you some trouble in recent years. Before answering your letter I had to wait for my engineers to make a thorough study of the problem and they have just completed their report.
These studies show that the northern part of the runway (the first 1,500 feet) should be entirely rebuilt, at an approximate cost of $315,000, which would be very difficult to justify at present if one considers that the kind of aircraft flown by Fecteau Transport Aerien, namely the British Islander, may operate in all safety on the other part of the runway which is still in good condition.
When one of our aircraft used it about one month ago, someone did notice that the northern part of the runway was not in very good condition though quite safe for several types of planes. However, to be on the safe side, we propose to move the threshold of runway 16 southward, making thus a runway 3,500 feet long, which is enough for many aircraft including the DC-3.
And I happened to make a representation in this House about aircraft that are used for bush flights, to fight

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleagues.
Concerning the Roberval airport, I know the minister is concerned about it, since the project is on his desk. He will have the assistance of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who committed himself during the last election campaign; I sent him a photograph, a photograph of him taken on the Roberval landing strip when he promised that he would personally make sure that the landing strip is rebuilt. I feel the Minister of Finance has made a tremendous commitment. I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) not to hesitate, to go and see the Minister of Finance and have him keep his word.
Now, I wish to call the attention of the House to another airport now being built. I have delivered to the minister personally the specifications of the Dolbeau airport. A letter was sent to the minister on January 16.1 believe that this letter is on file at his office; I do not know who was the incumbent minister at the time. The letter reads as follows:
Two years ago, a committee was set up by the city of Dolbeau for the purpose of developing the local airport at Saint-Methode, county of Roberval. That airport is located in the geographic centre of Roberval county and was first built by the Department of National Defence in the forties to be used in emergencies.
We submitted a request to your departmental officials and those officials paid us a visit to look into the technical merits of our request.
The purpose of our letter is to acquaint you with the situation and also to ask you to agree to our request when your officials put before you a positive recommendation.
The minister is aware of the situation; I spoke to him briefly concerning that report, which I handed him. That project is worth studying, especially as the city of Dolbeau owns that beautiful flat land. I believe that the minister has gone over the field which it is quite suitable. I do not know whether he has given a final reply to the city of Dolbeau which simply asked that the work be speeded up. It would be a good thing if we could get something by next summer. This field would be used mostly as a stopover for tourist planes, fishermen's and forest protection planes. An asphalt coating for this runway would not be too expensive and I honestly think that this would prove to be a genuine asset for our area. It would complete the air transportation system at Roberval. I am led to believe the minister is willing to look seriously into whatever is wrong with the Roberval airport. I hope, also, that a thorough

study will be made in connection with the Dolbeau airport and that the area will get something for next summer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the outcome of this afternoon's debate will be but surely certain facts will come out which will significantly help us, under whatever government, to follow a transportation policy which will truly meet our general needs.
It is normal and rather easy to criticize the government but if there is a concensus on general objectives it is not a total loss. I have been quite impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) who stated a number of truths I will elaborate on later.
But the basic truth which came out of this afternoon's debate-and I would like everyone to remember it-is that this country, which we call Canada and which is ours, probably could not exist without an adequate transportation system, without all the regions being interconnected and, economically speaking, without all the Canadian regions being able to communicate with the rest of the country.
Canada-and this is nothing new-is a large country which spreads from Halifax to Vancouver and into the far north and surely if instead of speaking of unity in abstract terms each of those great regions were interconnected, that would do more for unity than anything else.
Over the weekend-if memory serves me right I left Friday noon-I went to the Arctic region. I stopped over in Calgary; I went to Inuvik and to Yellowknife and by five o'clock Sunday I was back in Ottawa without being unduly tired. This means that with modern transportation it is possible to know physically this country. Besides, I have had the opportunity to say in the North that a country which is not settled, which is not developed is not a country which actually belongs to us. It is a country which stays somewhat alien because it is not integrated, it is not developed. Furthermore it feels very isolated not only from the rest of Canada but from the whole continent.
We have today modern means of making it possible for Canadians to go out of their regional isolation. And this is very important. But at the same time, the fact that these modern means are put at the disposal of the public inevitably creates frictions.
There are things which were not accepted 50 or 100 years ago for the simple reason that what happened in Ontario, in Vancouver or in Nova Scotia was not known. But communications today enable us not only to be informed but also to travel very quickly from one place to another, so that we get the physical impression that this country is really ours and that we have the means not only to exploit it but also to enjoy it.
I think that this is the basic idea, both from the point of view of national unity and from the economic and social points of view. In fact, it is important that we have what my friend the hon. member of Vegreville (M. Mazankow-ski) called a policy of integrated transport and that, of course, even if we cannot do everything at a moment's notice, we know all the same the short and long term objectives so that Canadians know that in 5, 10, 15 or 20 years this country will really be crisscrossed by adequate transport and communication systems.
March 20, 1973

Mr. Speaker, I think that transportation in Canada is a tremendous subject and I also think that it is extremely important, even vital. It is probably one of the greatest problems in Canada: a problem of communications and a problem of transport. I simply regret that, especially in the case of the official opposition, no suggestions have been put forward.
I listened very closely to my good friend from Vegreville and I shall do like him, that is, tell him he is a nice fellow and then tell him unpleasant things. That is what he did to me; I am quite willing to play the same little game. I am sure he is sincere, but I told myself while listening to him: surely, at some point or other he will speak of transport, and tell us the Progressive Conservative party has pondered the problem. But no, he took pleasure in counting the times I gave evasive answers in the House. I shall give him the statistics: he will see that even on that score he is wrong. Anyway, it is all very amusing. As the new Minister of Transport, I am quite willing to be made fun of, because I intend to feel free to do so too.
In any event, I am sorry the Progressive Conservative party has nothing to offer with regard to such an important subject. Still the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) honours me by being here this afternoon. He will speak after me; I am therefore taking chances. I checked to see whether between 1958 and 1962 the Progressive Conservative party had really drawn up an integrated transport policy for Canada, but I found nothing. Doubtless he can tell me where I can find it, that we might be able to follow the pillar of light that got lost in the mists of time.
We see that there are problems. The most obvious of these is the problem of transportation costs, especially in western Canada. I am as amazed as anyone in the House when I come across freight rates that are higher for goods transported to Regina than for those transported to Vancouver or elsewhere. I can understand it in the context of the capitalist system, but that does not make it any more sensible; anyone who believes in profits and in the private enterprise system knows that any company tries for the highest yield that the market can absorb. And that is the only valid explanation, because from a rational point of view, there is no other. It is not just surprising, even if an explanation can be found within the context of the present system, but it is also not very rational in my opinion, it is even a provocation, to set up such a system.
That, Mr. Speaker, is why, in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and immediately following it, I said that as soon as I had the time and as soon as the western premiers were free, I would be prepared to meet with them. They postponed the meeting with the representatives of the railway companies, not out of bad faith, Mr. Speaker, but because they wanted to have an opportunity to get together. I believe they are meeting on March 28 or 29; I do not remember the exact date. Then they will be prepared to meet the representatives of the railway companies, upon which they will be ready to meet me to talk about precisely this problem of freight rates and transportation costs in the West. And I trust that, with everyone's co-operation, we will manage to
Transportation Policy
improve the present situation, which is frequently intolerable.
We have been trying for years to do the same thing in the Maritime provinces, with the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, and also with a Transport Committee with jurisdiction over all the Atlantic provinces, which looks into all their problems. I am meeting the premiers of the Maritime provinces on April 9 to discuss how we can remedy the freight rate situation in that region. Unfortunately, I cannot do more than this; it will be the first chance I have to take action and, since our friends of the official opposition are tying us down and trying to paralyze government action as much as they can, of course, I have to ask the premiers of the Maritimes to come and meet me in Ottawa. Otherwise, I cannot see how I could do it, except on Sunday morning before Mass-for those who attend it. In any case, there is a problem in the Maritimes. There is no doubt about that. And it is a problem to which we are trying to find a solution.
Mr. Speaker, let me get away from regional demagogy for a while; one should not think that the one and only problem in the Maritimes is a transportation problem and that everything else would automatically straighten out if this problem were solved. Unfortunately, this is not true. How I would like it to be so, because the moment a solution would be found to the transportation problems, all the problems in those provinces would be solved, but that is not true. Still, we are going to make an effort in that direction.
Concerning this effort, we want it to be in co-operation with the provinces, with those concerned. If members think that by developing a general policy and applying it to the country in general, they will have solved the problem, they are mistaken, because they will only have given rise to new grievances, since the regions want the solutions we bring to really answer their respective needs.
This is why, when we conducted a study on urban transport in Winnipeg, for example, we worked jointly with the province and the municipality. We paid three quarters of the costs-I think it was $500,000-to determine whether it would be advisable to relocate the railway tracks in a city, whether to put them under or above ground, and what would be the best solution with regard to the impact on urban development. I hope that the example of Winnipeg will be followed in other cities, because the same problem occurs in many Canadian cities with railway tracks running through them and hindering the normal urban development. We are dealing with the matter and are making considerable progress.
I should now like to refer to the Maritime provinces. For example, we are told: "What are you doing about coastal traffic and the findings of the Darling report"? I will tell you what is being done with the Darling report after meeting with the Atlantic premiers who fear that the implementation of that report's recommendations would result in increased transportation costs, because, of course, foreign coasting vessels in the Maritimes often have extremely underpaid crews and do not have to bear the same costs as Canadian ships.
Nevertheless, I believe we should take every possible means in order that coastal shipping be done by Canadian ships and crews. But before we can make such a decision,

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
I want to be sure that the Maritime provinces concerned are not only consulted but are satisfied, that their position will not be worse than it is now.
That is one of the problems facing us that we are trying to solve under a comprehensive program.
Reference was made to Canada's air policy, it is not an easy thing, to be sure, for this is a vast country and there are grievances against the companies. Certainly we are one of the few countries-apart from the United States- with two great intercontinental companies competing with one another at times, which obviously raises a real problem. How can it be solved? We are looking into the matter. Can they really live side by side and develop harmoniously? Time will tell, but the department is looking into the matter and the least we can do-and I believe that is what the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre said-is to act in such a way that the state-owned company, or even the other one, are not placed in such a competitive position that sooner or later Canadians taxpayers will have to pay the cost of that apparent luxury of having two big companies serving Europe and the whole world.
What is important and fundamental for us in Canada is that we should seek abroad our share of the market, that Canadians should be able to go almost anywhere in the world on Canadian carriers and that foreigners should be able to come to this country with our own airlines, which also applies to air cargo. That is what is important if we want to prosper. In principle, I see no objection to the operation of two air carriers, but I object to their destroying one another, with the taxpayer ending up picking up the tab. But if they are wise they can share the traffic and try to make the most of the dual system. That is worth considering. I tried to understand the policy of the Progressive Conservative party on that matter. I already know that of my hon. friend from Regina-Lake Centre. I did not understand that of our Progressive Conservative friends, but I suppose they will tell us what they think sooner or later.
We have tried to reach new agreements with some countries. We recently signed an agreement with West Germany which not only gives us access to two more German cities, but also gives us what is known as the "fifth freedom of the air", in other words the right to leave Germany for destinations in other countries. We have also signed an agreement with China, under which CP Air will serve Peking and-
