speechtext: When will that be?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
In due course, as the right hon. member used to say when he was on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, we are trying to develop our air transport companies; we are trying to have them serve as many 
places as possible, and thus get their share of the passenger and freight markets.
All this brings us to discuss the problem of airports in Canada. Ever since it has been my honour and my great pleasure to be the Minister of Transport, I have heard talk of nothing but airports. As I was saying recently, I used to think Canada consisted of ten provinces, with two official languages and various ethnic groups. I had a very naive notion of Canada; when you get down to it, that is not Canada. Our country is split into two groups: those who want airports and those who do not want them. And I am caught between the two.
Aviation has developed during my generation; when I started working several years ago and a friend made a plane trip, we used to go down to his place to hear about his trip, because at that time very few people travelled by plane. When I was a little boy in Champlain and we heard the sound of a plane, we used to run out to see that wonderful thing. It was extraordinary, but that kind of poetry has disappeared.
The plane is no longer a bird, no longer an expression of human intelligence but a monster threatening the lives of people, a kind of cancer, and some people are afraid of it.
When there was talk of building an airport in the province of Quebec, it was not because we were behind or because another approach was being taken, but because people fought for it throughout the province. Some wanted it at Drummondville, others elsewhere.
Toronto no longer wanted it. The people in Pickering want the airport to be built elsewhere-and I understand them-but those are decisions we have to make.
In Vancouver, where they have had an airport for less than 30 years, adding another runway has created a great problem.
Now what does that mean? That means simply-and I accept it readily-that we did not expect those new reactions from people who are not necessarily enthused over the fact that planes will be landing close to their homes. People want reasons; it is true that the sound produced by modern airplanes is a great inconvenience. There will have to be a new approach about people, that is to say that before making such important decisions we undoubtedly need more consultation and information so that people will not consider progress as a threat to their peace, their security and even their life.
Mr. Speaker, we will continue to have airports in Canada as long as I will be Minister of Transport because I would be making a great mistake if, except for very serious reasons, I were to deprive a city such as Vancouver of an adequate airport. I know that the coming generation would not forgive us.
Our territory is becoming more and more settled. This is now the case in the United States; one day soon we will hear about a report presented to the president of the United States which will reveal how shortsighted people were not to set land aside for airports.
There is one thing that we could not do without in 1972 and even less in 1980: the aircraft and especially the jet which is here to stay. Maybe some hon. members still enjoy the poetry of the bus, and so on, but I believe that
March 20, 1973

for practical reasons the great majority of Canadians prefer flying.
Our friend from Regina-Lake Centre spoke about research in the field of transport but he took inconsistent position: he referred to the STOL aircraft. He said that was designed to encourage private enterprise. That is not true.
With the STOL system, we wish to make an experiment not to establish a permanent system between Montreal and Ottawa but to show that this system is possible. If it is, it means that there would be an external market for STOL aircraft which would secure jobs for Canadians and allow our economy to develop in this particular area.
Now, the hon. gentleman bares a grudge against the fact that, very often, our aircraft industry is controlled by Americans. I agree with him. He only needs to ask his friend, Premier Schryer of Manitoba who is facing the same problem with the aircraft companies settling in Winnipeg.
I am not here to change the whole system but to see that development in the aircraft industry meets our needs. So, the STOL experiment is a research investment and we are trying to show that it will serve the travellers while providing an outlet on the international market. Furthermore, I have once again heard about the hydrofoil which cost I do not know how many million dollars. But if our friend from Regina really believes in research and thinks it necessary to find new transportation means, he must not forget that many million dollars will have to be spent and possibly for nothing. The very principle of research itself is that you cannot help but work without knowing exactly what is really going to happen. We know in what direction we are working, but we do not know what the result will be.
We simply have to recall the two scientists of the United States Bell Company, who have discovered the transistor principle. They had carried out research for many years and one day they invented the first transistor which possibly cost many million dollars. But when they found the secret, it revolutionized the world.
In order to deal with almost all subjects, I shall say a word about our maritime policy. What are we doing in this field? We are trying to make our harbours efficient. We know, for instance, that there is a change in the field of maritime transportation where they have started using containers as well as huge tankers. We are endeavouring to equip our ports to cope with these changes. So, it is incorrect to say that we are not considering these things. On the contrary, we do consider them, as we did concerning the Vancouver and St. John harbours.
We are now considering two other harbours, probably in eastern Canada, and more particularly in the Mari-times, because we know that the future of transport is in that field. In fact, we will see before long some huge cargo ships, container ships, or tankers in our harbours. And we have on the east coast an asset which is entirely ours.
There are, in fact, no deep-water harbours in the United States. Oif our east coast, we have them, namely in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, near the mouth of the St. Lawrence and that is a tremendous resource which we are striving to develop as rationally as
Transportation Policy
possible. To benefit by that advantage, we must not only resort to dredging in certain places but we must also equip ourselves with port facilities geared to the future.
I shall now broach the subject of northern development. At the present time, it is not all just talk; we are extending the highway along the Mackenzie corridor. I have just returned from a visit to that region and I feel there are terrific developments there. They have modern airports. Actually, I officiated at the inauguration of two of them, where there have been extensions. They have been provided with facilities, electronic technology and equipment for the purpose of increasing air security in the region.
For instance, we shall soon be setting up systems called VORDME-Very	High Frequency Omnidirectional
Range-in Yellowknife, Inuvik, Frobisher Bay, Resolute Bay and Whitehorse, as well as distance-gauging instrument in order that air traffic in the north may offer a maximum of security.
The Northern Transportation Company Limited has met with great success this year; besides everybody wants to buy it.
Then again, Mr. Speaker, we are faced with the problem of the Canadian Transport Commission. I hope that I shall have the opportunity of discussing it further, because often we are told: You claim that Parliament cannot do anything about it. I think that the hon. member for Vegreville has been mistaken because if he checks the blues he will see that nobody ever claimed that Parliament had no jurisdiction over the Canadian Transport Commission. He probably meant "the government" because Parliament has jurisdiction over that commission. There is no doubt that should Parliament decide to change-
The House of Commons has authority over the Canadian Transport Commission.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: It does not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Of course, it has; we can change the law.

However, being the government, we cannot give instructions to the Canadian Transport Commission. Only in a few cases appeals can be directed to the minister, such as the granting of permits. Otherwise, right or wrong, the House of Commons has legislated on the status quo of this body, as for better or for worse there has been legislation on the autonomy of the CBC, the CRTC, the Polymer Corporation Limited and others. This indicates there is some kind of Canadian tradition whereby some activities are safeguarded even against government action. If this concept were to be a matter of doubt, I am quite willing to discuss it very freely, Mr. Speaker, because I have my own opinions on this subject. However, I had the law applied as it is and I have assumed responsibility for the commission as it has been established. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, I do not recall that, between the years 1958 to 1962, under the Progressive Conservative administration, there were important amendments to the National Trans-

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
portation Act to empower the government to give instructions to this commission.
There have been a few brief comments about charter planes. Naturally every time changes have been made- this is the second time a change has occurred in this field-there has to be a five or six month readjustment period. On the other hand, the opposition members have been really helpful in this area. Cases were submitted to me and I had some changes made. No doubt there will be other matters to look into shortly and hon. members will certainly not hesitate to tell me about them.
At any rate, I have dealt with only part of the department's operations. To say in very broad and vague terms that the department has done nothing, has devised nothing and produced nothing is somewhat exaggerated. To tell us that we have not acted quickly enough, that we have made mistakes, that there are better solutions, that is a bit too thick! The opposition members really are a little too secretive; having once pretended they were robbed of some of their ideas, they seem to put away in a safe their few other remaining ideas, but why do they not sport them in the open? I for one should be happy to hear them state an integrated transport policy as they conceive it, as well as a subsidy policy also the way they see it. Now the spokesman for the official opposition perhaps was not prepared to do it, but the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), former prime minister, for his part, is prepared. No doubt he will be in a position to tell me what I have to do in the department in order to have Canada effectively provided with the best possible transportation system, so that we might be able to meet the needs of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that a sincere effort is being made in the department, which includes the Canadian Marine Transportation Administration, the Canadian Surface Transportation Administration, the Northern Transportation Company Limited, the Arctic Transportation Agency, Air Canada, a Crown corporation, the Canadian National, the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, the National Harbours Board. The department is extremely complex and if ever the hon. member for Vegreville becomes Minister of Transport-when he is very old-he will be able to see how easy it is to harass a Minister of Transport since he can never know everything, be aware of everything that may go on in such a complicated and altogether important box.
We must solve the transportation problems of the Mari-times and the west and we must ensure that our air transport companies develop normally. We also have a harbour policy as well as all the necessary elements to further the progress of Canada and I think had this resolution been serious in the least, it would have given rise to a really useful debate on the subject of transportation.
This motion so far has only given the opposition an opportunity to make a few jokes-I thought one of them was funny-and allowed my good friend from the Lake St. John area to speak about the Roberval airport. I think I shall not take up the time of the House to comment on this, but I shall see the hon. member and we shall certainly agree eventually on this question.

Mr. Speaker, I like to see parliament live. I enjoy a good debate and a contribution to the debate from whatever quarter it is made. For that reason I am always fond of hearing the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) who, with a minimum of argument, makes a maximum of speech. The House lives when he speaks because he is actually debating. However, I think his speech may be well summed up by the words he used earlier when he said: "Whenever we decide to act we will let you know in due course". We found out today that "due course" has not yet arrived. We had a dissertation on the subject of national unity to which I want to make passing reference. The minister claimed that little or nothing has been advanced except by the hon. member from the province of Quebec, who I thought made a quite thoughtful contribution and one which indicated there is indeed a degree of diminuition of morale in respect of the Canadian National Railway that can be attributable only to the fact that there is not now and is apparently not in anticipation a national transportation policy.
Before I go into detail, I must congratulate the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) for what I thought was an exceptionally well reasoned speech on a
March 20, 1973

subject which needs to be discussed. The minister touched on no part of the resolution. He did not touch on the suggestion that there should be an integrated over-all national transportation policy. The hon. member noted the inadequacy of the ministerial response to Canada's transportation problems, and the minister's speech has fully established that. He deplored the government's failure to recognize that Canadian transport is vital to Canadian unity, regional equality and resource development. This represents a cogent criticism of the policies of this government, or the lack of policies if I might use a better description.
I have known the minister through the years. I remember when I was Prime Minister he belonged to a party other than the one to which he belongs today. That was before the three horsemen of the Apocalypse found their way into the Liberal party. I admire his capacity for speech. I admire the enthusiasm the minister can work up in making generalities very attractive. However, when you come to finally analyzing what he said, the question becomes a simple one.
For a period of years, he was Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. During that period of years there was no endeavour on the part of the minister or the government to do anything regarding regional development on the Prairies, for instance. They were forgotten. That is one of the reasons the government received such a shellacking on the Prairies in the last federal election. One would have thought there would have been some hope of reformation. The minister spent hundreds of millions of dollars in the area in which it pleased him to spend it, and he forgot western Canada almost completely.
He talked of national unity, but I will not deal with those speeches that he made immediately after the election when overcome by surprise, annoyance and frustration, he dared to suggest that anybody who criticized the government and any of its policies was undermining Canadian unity. That was not in keeping with the fine reputation that I had built around him. Some of the statements that he made were despicable, and there can be no other way to describe them. He intimated that because I disagree with the views he holds, apparently I become somewhat of an enemy of the state. That is not in keeping with the parliamentary tradition, and that is not the kind of argument that one would have expected from him. But he was annoyed, he was exasperated, he was overcome with surprise at the defeat that had hit the government. So, he had to attack.
To begin with, I say to him that I hope the same disregard of the prairie provinces and other parts of Canada, such as the Maritimes, will not become an epidemic with him as he now finds himself in a new portfolio. I do not know why the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) shifts these ministers around. There were the four-the hon. gentleman himself and-but I cannot keep up with the portfolios. I do not want such a high degree of unanimity, Mr. Speaker, but apparently it covers the whole House. Does the minister forget that it was under that government that expansion of the production of rape-seed in Saskatchewan was made possible, and in the other provinces to a lesser degree, by providing the support of the party as a whole for a private bill introduced by Reynold Rapp, which brought rapeseed under the Crows-nest Pass Agreement, and therefore not only made possible the expansion of rapeseed production but put the profit on every pound of rapeseed into the pockets of western farmers? I mention just those two things. I could mention others as well.
Just by way of example, what is the minister going to do about freight rates? What is the government going to do? It is not enough for him to say that, "Some time, somewhere, some place we will tell you about it in the future." Niddle-noddle is exactly the attitude he displayed today- neither this nor that, but words mounted in great eloquence. There was no answer to the proposition placed before the House by the hon. member for Vegreville in a remarkably astute, able, and well delivered speech.

The minister spoke of northern development. Did he find any when he was up there that was not brought into affect under my administration, or as a result of the policies of this party during our period of office? What did we do for transportation? We provided assistance to every province in Canada, $71 million over a period of five years either for the building of highways to resources, or in those provinces that did not have mineral resources, for tourist encouragement and the like.
What did we do, Mr. Speaker? Well, I remember all the criticism, I remember the Liberal party going up and down the length of Canada when I spoke of building roads into the north. They said it was a dream, that what I had in mind was to build highways from igloo to igloo. So original was that, that when I looked up the debates of 1874 respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway I found that the Liberal party of that day said "from wigwam to wigwam." That was the only change made in 80 years. There was no consideration given to the north.
I remember when we brought forward legislation to provide the guarantee for the building of the railway from near Grimshaw, Alberta, to Pine Point, how they jeered. You could almost describe it as cynical disregard for the facts. Today that railroad is one of the most lucrative in all Canada, and has opened up northern resources to an extent that was even dreamt of by us, although we realized the great potentialities of the north. We followed that policy in northern Canada, in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. But what did we hear today from the minister? He said, "I am going to build a couple of airport warning signals. We are really thinking about it." Mr. Speaker, no minister ever got an appreciation of northern development by flying to Inuvik and back in 40 hours. Look the situation over up there. There is so much that can be done, so much to do, and so much that will bring new wealth to Canada.
When I rose today, Mr. Speaker, it was not to deal particularly with these matters, but to discuss for a while a matter of very deep concern to me, one that deserves the consideration of the House. It has to do with a subject that is being discussed now all over again. How are we going to transport the oil and the gas of northern Canada to the markets? There have been a number of alternative plans. One is by ship, a most dangerous potentiality to environmental pollution. There have been a number of suggestions that there should be pipelines. Where? There are two different routes.
I suggest to the Minister of Transport that he should fully look into a question that I raised in the House on February 15, and to which I am going to direct my remarks. As recorded at page 1311 of Hansard I asked:
In view of the fact that one of the most important economic matters facing our country today is the question of the transport of oil, gas and so on from the Yukon and Alaska I wish to ask the Minister of Transport whether there is a task force now operating to the end that problems of environmental difficulty and so on will not come into being should the suggestion be accepted to build a railway from the north having its initial terminus in Saskatchewan...
But I am not going to argue that, even though with complete objectivity I would like to see Prince Albert in that position. There was not a word on that today. On February 15, the minister said:

I should like to ask him whether or not the most appropriate route would not be through Saskatchewan, and what is the estimate today of the cost of such a railway through British Columbia and Alberta with the terminus I mentioned in Saskatchewan. Have any such estimates been made?

I thank my colleagues and all hon. members. The answer given by the minister was:
I have not yet met with the Premier of Saskatchewan. I intend to do so.
I would think there would be no more ideal time than the present. This is one of those things that cannot but add cement to the rather uncertain relationship that prevails now. The minister added:
I think we will have to study the whole question of transportation in the north in consultation with the provinces.
What has been done, Mr. Speaker? What has been done in the last month by the government in this connection?
The minister also said:
Whenever those studies are complete I will be happy to make a report to the hon. gentleman.
I do not expect to be here until eternity, Mr. Speaker, and I simply ask: when are we going to get this report? Any time the minister would like, 1 am prepared to give him my place to enable him to answer that question. What is he doing except talking?
When the oil field in Alaska was discovered some four years ago there was no suggestion of railway transportation. There was silence on the part of railway companies. There was silence as the icebreaker Manhattan chopped its way through the inland passage north of the Arctic circle. Even when Boeing proposed flying the North Slope crude oil out of Alaska there was no response from the railroads. I agree with what has been said today by members on both sides of this House about Canadian railway companies. They do not give a tinker's damn for the average Canadian, or for providing transportation. They have reaped the benefits, taken the cream and now they want to leave ghost towns and provide the kind of service in the Chicoutimi area of the province of Quebec that was referred to earlier today.
Transportation Policy
In the spring of 1971 the Canadian Institute of Guided Ground Transport initiated an engineering, economic and environmental feasibility study of a railway to carry Arctic oil to market. Later, this study was expanded to include the transportation of liquid natural gas. The study was prompted by an earlier preliminary analysis by the Transportation Research Institute at Carnegie-Mellon University. With the co-operation of Carnegie-Mellon, the CNR, Canadian National Telecommunications, PROCOR Ltd., Canadian Pacific and Catalytic Enterprises Ltd., 16 professionals associated with CIGGT completed the oil transportation feasibility study. The report, which I have read carefully and which is available, concluded that such a railroad is technically and operationally feasible and appears to be financially attractive. There were various proposals. One proposed route would start at Prudhoe Bay, proceed along the Arctic slope to the Mackenzie delta and then southeast along the Mackenzie River valley for a distance of some 1,200 miles.
What is being done? What did the task force decide upon, if anything? What is the government doing today to consider the matter of railway transportation? Such a railroad would, according to estimates, require an average employment of 5,000 people for construction over a 5 J-year period. It would do much to open the north; it would mean that thousands of people would establish themselves in the north in the same way as they have already been established by the U.S.S.R. in similar latitudinal areas of that country. It would mean a great increase in population in the north. It would bring about not only direct employment but indirect employment. The economic benefits would be substantial for all of us in this country.
The figures which I have indicate that the railway would require some 360 six-axle locomotive units and
11,000	tank cars of 94-ton capacity. It would require 20 trains per day of 168 cars, towed by five locomotive units, to move the necessary 2 million barrels of oil. The railway would be double-tracked, with advanced communications.
What is being done in that area? There will always be some environmental difficulties. They are inevitable no matter what mode is used to transport this oil to market. The real environmental question is simply, which mode of transportation and which route can permit the required movement of oil at acceptable economic cost within an acceptable time period and with a minimum of environmental cost? That subject deserves attention.
Let me now speak of Arctic pipelines. The great difficulty with oil pipelines in the Arctic is that they must operate at high temperatures, between 150 and 180 degrees. Buried pipelines cannot be insulated to prevent permafrost melting under such conditions. Elevated pipelines are expensive and pose additional environmental problems. A railway does not generate heat to these high temperatures and accordingly need not melt the permafrost: the thick surface layer of crushed rock ballast is good insulation and thus it is easier to prevent ground damage than it is in the case of a pipeline or even a road. As well, wildlife will benefit if there is a careful selection of route.

This could be done, Mr. Speaker. People used to say that the Hudson Bay Railway would never be built. Macdonald predicted the Hudson Bay Railway when he spoke in Regina in July, 1885. He predicted routes into the north. He said that there would be within very few years a railway to Prince Albert, the most northerly place in the territories at that time. He was right: it came in 1891. He had predicted, as well, the Hudson Bay Railway but that did not come about until Sir Wilfrid Laurier launched it in 1908.
Economically, the effects of a railway would be entirely positive, as I have said. One of the major secondary benefits would be peripheral mineral development, that is, resource development and the creation of jobs. These beneficial effects would be felt in every part of our country. We now know that the north is actually the safety deposit box of those things that through the years will assure us that freedom will survive. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to this proposal. For some reason, the bureaucrats do not want anything like this, and when the bureaucrats do not want anything they throw cold water on it. But the time has come for the government to act and follow policies along lines adopted by the administration I had the honour to lead, which effectively opened up the north for the first time.
There is a tremendous challenge in this area. To the minister I say, if he wants to take his place in the history of our country he must challenge the certainties of bureaucrats who, having determined that what they have in mind is best, refuse to face the greater issue of the future of Canada. I ask him to give consideration to my proposal, because I find more and more that parliament does not have the effect it used to have. The bureaucrats prepare the menu and the minister brings it in and says, "Eat." Amendments are denied; legislation is pushed through, even when there is a majority, by closure. In conclusion I say this to the minister, as I said at the beginning: when he speaks, this great institution lives, because he has that infinite capacity, with the knowledge that he has, of being able to speak in such a way that the House of Commons once more becomes a vital place.

Providing for national security and ensuring adequate sources of assistance in the event of national disasters, physical and economic.
The foregoing are in large measure the points at which transportation policy-making begins and to which it must continually refer. They emphasize the need to analyse transportation problems systematically so that their constituent elements can be related to the elements of our objectives and to our broad principles. Determining the implications of these relationships is crucial to the framework for approaching this task.
Patently, it is important that we as a nation identify and articulate our transportation objectives and secure for them a broad degree of public understanding and acceptance. Achieving the necessary degree of acceptance will be no small task, given the large role of the private sector in transportation, the independence of transportation regulatory bodies, the sharing of transportation responsibilities by many levels of government, and the confusing barrage of conflicting information that seers of every description hurl upon an already confused public.

speechtext:
Railways have played an important role in the development of Canada and the growth of its urban centres. The increasing need to provide for urban mobility to meet population growth in Canada's urban areas has led, however, to a situation where railway facilities are in many ways a troublesome presence which interferes with urban mobility and safety, occupies valuable sites, presents formidable obstacles to desirable directions and patterns of urban growth, and contributes significantly to the blight of land.
Accordingly, the federal government is presently considering the extension of financial aid toward the solution of railway-highway grade-crossing problems. The whole question has recently been studied in Winnipeg in a project jointly funded by federal, provincial and municipal governments and the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. It is hoped that legislation will soon be introduced which will provide a mechanism to assist in the development of rail relocation or traffic rerouting schemes. A railway grade-crossing fund with annual expenditures of $15 million to $20 million is presently in existence. It is expected that new legislation will appreciably raise the ceiling of such expenditures over the years.
I would now like to quote from a submission made to the government by the Canadian Federation of Mayors

and Municipalities which met with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of the cabinet yesterday, March 19.1 quote their submission as follows:
A study undertaken by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities of some 85 transportation plans from some 25 Canadian cities during the last ten years showed that only ten had been completed while others are in some stage of implementation and many have been allowed to die on the drafting boards. In many cases, plans prepared by private consultants could not stand the test of public and political scrutiny. The majority, however, failed because of an inadequate tax base at the municipal level.
There is no greater challenge facing our age than coping with the surging tide and demands of urbanization as reflected in our transportation requirements.
There is need for a full partnership, full co-operation, full involvement and a full understanding of the need to reallocate responsibility and resources in a manner which allows each level of government to carry out its share of the responsibility of making our communities the places of hope, opportunity and progress that we wish them to be.
It is for these reasons that the municipalities of Canada seek the appointment of a municipal representative to the commissioner level of the Canadian Transport Commission.
Mr. Speaker, this is in line with the throne speech and with the meeting between the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), the provincial premiers and the Western Economic Conference slated to take place on July 15, 1973. The regulatory field of transportation is never one which is popular with all the people or with all facets of the transportation industry. In this area the challenge has been to establish and to maintain, wherever possible, economically viable and competitive transportation systems. More often than not, however, public subsidies have been and will continue to be required for reasons that range from national unity to the basic needs of our people. While the trend has been, in most competitive fields, toward modernization and centralization, this will not be allowed to progress to the point of services being eliminated or reduced on purely economic grounds.
On the other hand, we must continue to look to the needs of the future. In co-operation with other levels of government, progress is being achieved. Municipal transportation systems are being tested on a practical basis using known technology. At the same time, we are actively involved in research programs which in the future could affect all modes of transportation.
While time does not permit a complete discussion of the complex field of transportation, I can assert that our policies in this field are aimed not only at filling the needs of today but they are also looking toward the needs of tomorrow. None of our programs in the field of transportation will be successful if the people they are to serve do not participate in their development. This is an area where elected representatives at all levels of government should openly express the views of the people they represent. This is what the Minister of Transport is attempting to do: he and his department are studying all aspects of their responsibilities. I assure the House and the Canadian people of the sincerity of the minister. Of all the people capable of doing this job, he is the best.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject this evening is transportation. The problem is the lack of leadership. The answer is common sense. The need is for a completely new, imaginative approach to transportation in Canada-in short, an entirely new transportation policy. Transportation is the one area which affects the lives of all Canadians. Basic legislation in this area is a makeshift, patch job over old ideas that were barely adequate when introduced. Successive ministers of transport over the past ten to 12 years have failed miserably to produce leadership or a cohesive on-going plan of action.
Aware that my colleagues will be dealing with specific regional problems, I intend to cover generally some of the areas of concern to those of us in Ontario. No matter where one looks, the lack of future planning is evident. On water, we find harbours that are as antiquated as the pork-barrel method of appointing commissioners to the harbours boards. Not only are the harbours not integrated into the over-all transportation system, but they frequently fail properly to serve the recreational needs of the community of which they are part. With harbours a blight on many waterfronts, the harbours boards perpetuate a style and system even less adequate than the government which created them.
In the air, we have seen the government play power politics with people over airports, and all at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. We end up with two airports where one was obviously adequate, with none where one is desperately needed and easily provided, with extensions of airports at terrible cost to people and the environment. Obvious planning just a short time ago would have avoided all these problems. It is my personal opinion that a second airport in the Toronto region is absolutely uncalled for, unnecessary and an affront to common sense. I am proud to belong to a party where I can take this stand, knowing I will be listened to and not forced to hew the party line, in this case a Liberal party line-a line of obvious fiscal and environmental insanity.
Airlines are being forced to service areas other than the highest population density areas where the majority of the travelling public originates. Passengers from some areas frequently have to travel the same airspace twice to a destination because of inadequate service. Foul-ups of all kinds are the order of the day, and passenger service is
26087-7J
Transportation Policy
frequently the last requisite of a change in policy. Canadians are still forced to pay more for travel in their own country, on their own government-owned airline, than they do to leave their country on their own or any other airline. These and the new charter regulations make a mockery out of common sense. Already the new advance booking charter rules are being broken. The ABC rules mean "Any Body Can", and they do.
In the private and industrial flying sector, the situation is worse. Millions of dollars are spent annually on searches for lost aircraft. A portion of that money would provide a network of radio beams which would definitely go a long way toward doing away with the basic cause of accidents. I could not agree more with the many private pilots who claim that the cost of the so-called art at the major airports across Canada would easily pay for a good guidance system.
Truck transport is such a complete shemozzle in Canada that it is hard to know where to start. Lack of uniform licensing codes between provinces puts carriers in this field at a distinct disadvantage to trains. Railways buying out trucking lines with taxpayers' money to compete against other trucking firms owned by those same taxpayers seems to me the height of a ridiculous situation. The lack of leadership in this field is appalling.
Railways are the backbone of this country, both literally and figuratively. One might say that the country was formed to build a railroad and the building of the railroad formed the country. The railroads were built under adverse conditions, with equipment and techniques current then but antiquated in light of present day technology. They were built, however, with vigour by ingenious and daring men, and for one reason only-to serve a growing country.
The Liberal party has an interesting record in the area of railroads, one which continues to this day. In the late 1800s, after 18 years in opposition they denounced the fledgling Canadian Pacific Railway as an insane and ruinous defiance of North America's natural transport routes. Let me quote Mr. Donald Creighton, a Canadian historian of excellent repute, when he spoke of Mr. Laurier presenting the transport phase of the new Liberal nationalism.
They flung to the winds their old prudent and parsimonious misgivings about trans-continental railway enterprises; and with a swiftness and completeness acquired through frequent practice, they paid the last of the Conservative national policies-the policy of all-Canadian transport-the supreme compliment of adoption. Against all their grave warnings and gloomy predictions, the Canadian Pacific Railway had proved itself a tremendous success.
And the country grew and Mr. Laurier furthered this newly adopted policy.
-the Prime Minister's control of railway policy was absolute; and his great new railway enterprises moved steadily forward as lavish in execution as they had been grandiose in conception. The supervision of its construction was ostensibly entrusted by Laurier to a special National Trans-continental Railway Commission, composed of commissioners who knew nothing about railways and chaired by an ousted Liberal premier of Quebec-Simon Napoleon Parent, who regarded his appointment as a well-merited opportunity of serving the Liberal party and rewarding its political friends.

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
Continuing to quote Mr. Creighton when he spoke of Mr. Arthur Meighen who for a short while was Prime Minister of Canada:
He had never assumed that the Conservative policies of the nineteenth century were a sufficient answer to the problems of the twentieth. As a principal author of the Canadian National Railways he was strongly committed to state ownership.
Mr. Speaker, while I would love to go on and read much more of this fine book, I will end with this quote:
The Liberals had always preached a highly decentralized Canadian federalism. They had opposed Macdonald's national policies during the nineteenth century; and they had resisted most Conservative attempts to use the power of the state to carry out the characteristic national purposes of the twentieth.
What is the situation now? Carrying forward debts, not of their own making, the CNR has for a number of years been guilty of providing far less than adequate service, abandoning lines, reducing services, and of behaviour not becoming a well run railroad. A single example might be the much discussed passenger service between Barrie and Toronto. Made an election issue in an attempt to defeat the hon. member from York-Simcoe, $100,000 was promised by the Liberal government to test this service and, sure enough, the day after the election the test period began. Approximately a month later it stopped. Despite the fact that it carried almost exactly the proposed estimated daily number of passengers, it was termed a failure.
The charge supposedly paid by the federal government to the Canadian National Railways per coach was about $450 and yet two years earlier, in October, 1969, a private citizen, Mr. John Medcof of Barrie, rented the same coaches from the CN at $150 per coach and made a profit on his trial run. No attempt was made to tie in the experimental service with interconnecting buses or other existing services. This will give you some indication of the sincerity with which this government approaches the need for train commuter service in Ontario.
I must take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to read into the record again a question which the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) asked in the House of Commons on March 9 of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand):
Last June the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications recommended that all rail passenger services which were discontinued on November 1, 1970, in southwestern Ontario be re-established immediately and, second, that a joint study group of federal, provincial, and municipal officials and railway employees be established to determine a minimum rail passenger network at the lowest possible cost. This unanimous recommendation to parliament was signed by 20 members almost nine months ago. When is the minister going to take action on this matter?
The minister, in an equally long answer which said virtually nothing, blamed the fact that we had no railroads on the provincial government of Ontario and the government of metro Toronto. What the hon. member for Bruce wanted, of course, was service in an area where the federal government, if it wants to, can exercise complete control. The intercity passenger transport study, which the minister referred to as the Sobermann report, is an excellent research document and could well be the basis of future services, if it is ever used. One of the conclusions of this report is that in the 1970s-
The greatest benefit would be derived from improvements in the existing modes, such as on-time reliability (and consequent reduc-

tion in waiting time), passenger processing procedures, and rail improvements using existing trackage.
To this I add my own partial list of problems concerning commuter trains: the elimination of decent food service on trains is a cause of much complaint; the lack of adequate baggage handling facilities further discourages the travelling public; the lack of co-ordination of schedules with other services, and even other trains, confuses and further prohibits train travel; and the use of old-fashioned, uncooled, poorly ventilated coaches makes travel distasteful.
Mr. Speaker, may I make it abundantly clear, as I have in other instances of criticism on my part, that I am not condemning the employees of the Canadian National Railways or, for that matter, Air Canada. It is safe to say that I know almost a thousand of these employees personally, coming as I do from Belleville, the Rideau area headquarters of the Canadian National, and I know them to be conscientious, hard working individuals dedicated to their tasks, from the running trades to top management. No, Mr. Speaker, I lay the blame for this dreadful service right at the door of this government, and particularly the Minister of Transport. The Canadian National Railways and Air Canada are operators; they carry out the policy, or lack thereof, to the best of their ability. 'Where this policy is outdated or completely lacking we cannot possibly blame the operators for the deplorable conditions.
The common sense answer to most of the criticism I have levelled comes in the form of a new transportation policy. Just as Mr. Meighen was not prepared to accept the policies of the nineteenth century as being good enough for the twentieth, so the policies of the first half of the twentieth century are not relevant in the last half and, indeed, in this fast-paced world in which we live the policies of the 1960s are not readily acceptable in the 1970s.
In the field of research and development surely this country, which has a wealth of scientific and engineering talent, could develop a transportation system, if not better than, at least equal to the Japan national railways' system which operates trains at 150 m.p.h., or the French national railways' system which holds a rail speed record of 205 m.p.h. Do we really have to wait on a United States-based firm to spend years developing a train like the Turbo which balks at cold weather? Perhaps the U.S. or the Minister of Transport has not realized we have snow here in the winter.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I find it completely inconsistent that with the inadequacies I have pointed out, and with those outlined by my colleagues, we could possibly need an increase in the estimates for this year. I find, however, that the department has asked for an additional $224,303,000 and before these estimates can be passed we have a request for supplementary estimates of $107,308,580. The Canadian public will not long stand for this kind of extravagance. I am confident I speak for most taxpayers when I say that they are prepared to pay for services rendered, but to have budgets increased as these are, and still be presented with the level of service available today, is unpardonable.
Properly operated, the Department of Transport has, in my opinion, far greater potential for the reduction of
March 20,1973

regional disparity in the country than the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or any other gerrymandering program developed by this government. The key words are "properly operated". The Trudeau government has not to date demonstrated any ability or inclination to bring this department, or any other for that matter, into the present, never mind the future. My colleagues, under the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), are prepared to use the daring, imagination and initiative, inherently part of our party over the years, to bring about the changes required.
I see I have taken 15 minutes, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words on the subject of transportation, the issue having been brought before the House on the motion that we need an over-all, integrated national transportation policy. The mover of the motion points out that immediately upon this being found, it will solve the vital Canadian issues of unity, regional equality, the encouragement of resource development, the increase of international and domestic trade and the betterment of the urban and rural quality of life. This is an amazing proposition. Obviously, the search must be on in a very thorough way to find this tremendous national policy which would produce all these fantastic results.
The motion comes forward, in other words, in response to the fact that, in more precise words, the mover thinks there are improvements which could be made to our transportation policy. I do not suppose anyone would deny that. No matter who comes forward with a national transportation policy, there would be those who would suggest improvements to it.
Indeed, in this large country, with its low population, we are very dependent upon a national transportation system. It should not be assumed that some magic theory will suddenly produce a policy which will solve all our problems and create these great good things which the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), has decided would happen if a magic transportation policy were discovered. It is, of course, much easier to point to a specific problems, anomalies and difficulties than it is to establish cures which in fact not only deal with the problem but avoid creating new difficulties and new anomalies. That, of course, is an issue which is before us and will be before us for a long time.
It is rather ironic that a man from western Canada should move this motion at a time when the government, in the Speech from the Throne, has indicated a fundamental awareness of the need to examine transportation issues, to discuss these with the provincial governments and to produce results which will indeed further economic development in those areas of the country where that is the pressing need. It is, I suppose, fairly typical of these opposition motions and attacks that they usually come exactly in the area where a great deal of thinking and activity is gping on and where, indeed, they suspect we are likely to be moving toward new solutions and they want to appear to have been pressing for the improvements. That, of course, is nothing new and is not something we should be surprised about or should indeed argue against. That is
Transportation Policy
the role of an opposition. The question is whether it is being performed well or not very well.
The matter of a national transportation policy includes some pretty major questions about what we are doing and how we are doing it. There is also the rather important question of who will pay for what is done. No one should think that simple bookkeeping would change the fundamentals of that. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) seems to think that if we transferred the debts of the CNR from one account to another, that would bring about great gains. I think members should realize that the nature of the accounts, expenditures and the profit and income position, is understood and known. No simple transfer will make any difference at all.
The call for a new national transportation policy reminds one, as the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) has been reminded, of other national policies, particularly the national policy of Macdonald, which have had a part to play in the development of this country. Of course, the problems in respect of that national policy have created some anomalies and inequities such as in the tariff which the Tories built and maintained-which must be overcome by a new dynamic policy-which resulted from that structural development. Not only do we have the Speech from the Throne, but we have what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said when he was in the west, to the effect that he would be seeking a new national policy which would meet the aspirations of western Canada.
Many of us know, when we seek solutions to meet the aspirations of western Canada, they will be the same solutions which will meet the aspirations of other regions of the country, the Maritimes and eastern regions as well as the west. Solutions are the same for them because the transportation problem, the development problem and the population problem are often the same. Then we have hon. members saying that we need improvements. They point to things being done or which will no doubt be done in the next six months or a year and use those as examples. But they have not yet pointed out any co-ordinated and integrated national policy they would suggest be put in place, because when they have to come to specifics it is not that simple a job.
We have some examples of our progress in improving handling in the transportation system and the movement of products. Members opposite frequently have forgotten what has been done. I think, for instance, of the movement of grain in this country. Only a few weeks ago hon. members opposite stood up and asked when we would create a system of control or co-ordination for the movement of grain. They do not seem to realize that with the introduction of the block system in Winnipeg, and the co-operation which resulted from its operation and the introduction of a co-ordinator at the terminal at both ends for the movement of grain, we have in fact put in place an organized, efficient system for handling the movement of this extremely important product.
The only really difficult problems which hon. members can cite against the progress which has been made, against the performance of the handling of grain, comes when circumstances occur over which no one can have any or easy control. Among those which no one can control are weather conditions such as we had last year.

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
These unusual weather conditions impeded the movement of grain. Those over which one has control only with difficulty include the weapon of the strike, the industrial dispute which leads to a stoppage of work. This is not easy for anyone to solve, as we have seen in jurisdiction after jurisdiction, provincial and federal, in this country. Governments, whether they be Conservative and fail for months to manage to handle an elevator strike, or NDP, as in Saskatchewan, and have one of the worst years in the history of that province in terms of labour disputes, find it impossible to face up to the difficult problem of overcoming the decision of employees and of employers to disagree about how they will settle their arrangements between themselves.
These are examples which members opposite can cite as a temporary problem or failure of the system. But when these do not occur, the system works amazingly well; it works superbly. The system is capable of setting new records. It has allowed the handling of grain at a record level of millions of bushels beyond that forecast as possible with the same system only a short time before. That is a performance which is important and worth remembering.
We have, of course, in the area of the movement of grain the old and traditional friend, the Crowsnest pass rates. The Crowsnest rates have meant that the mover of grain has not been subject to a charge higher than that which existed in 1896, and he is not to this day. There are many people in western Canada who think this is a tremendous benefit to the west. The fact is, of course, that it has not worked out quite that way, because the cost of moving the product must be borne whether it is in freight rates or in some other form. In the system we face now there is the possibility of losses on products moved under those statutory rates being recovered from the rates which are charged on other products in the competitive area. Others very close to those who benefit from the statutory rates often bear the burden of the loss on those rates in the manner of recovery of the costs.
This is a fact which we should bear in mind and should not run away from when looking at the over-all question of how we can make more sensible our rate structure and the way in which it affects the development of the country. No one from the west could possibly ignore the anomalies which exist. Because of competitive conditions which may exist at the west coast or at some similar long distance point from the originating point, rates may be lower than those which are charged on the Prairies for the delivery of goods at an intermediate point.
The costing people can make a case for the fact that if you did not have lower rates, you would not move the goods and that the total cost on shorter hauls would in fact be higher. But it is at that point that we as a government clearly have to examine the question. These are the sort of questions which we are and will be examining as we look at what should be done and can be done to encourage development in regions such as western Canada where so much growth is possible and desirable for the good of the country as a whole.

When hon. members worry about the rail system's ability to move grain, they should take note of the fact that it has done an amazingly good job of placing at the required point the grain that is needed for sale by the Canadian Wheat Board. There have been new records every year. The selling and exporting of more grain than has been grown for two years in a row, and this in an orderly fashion, leads our buyers to have more confidence in our system than they have in that of some of our competitors.
The complaints which have existed about our system have paled into insignificance compared with the kind of problems which are being faced even in the United States, where there is lack of co-ordination and lack of knowledge of the amounts of grain which may be moved at any given point in time. They have had difficulties in organizing their system and in trying to get the grain to the port where the buyer wants it. They have had ten times more ships waiting compared with our worst periods, and this without weather problems but as a result of the difference in the nature of the systems.
We try to make sure that our system will carry the grain that ought to be carried. I should say to hon. members that there are some who still seem to think that our view that changes are needed in the handling system is somehow a criticism of its capacity to handle the grain at present. That criticism really misses the point. Capacity is one element, and there are some of us who believe, as I do, that we should have the capacity to move into export even more grain than we have moved in the two previous record years. But it is not the capacity of the system that is of major concern, because that can be added to by some minor modifications in the system. It is not the capacity of the system which is causing the examination of it and raising the question of change; it is the cost of the system.
I say time and time again to people in the prairie region interested in the grain industry that we should look at the money available to them as a total of what they will get for the goods they sell, plus what the treasury may make available for national policy reasons, and out of that sum anything that goes for cost will be their loss. If the cost is higher than necessary, then obviously we have a significant problem.
This is where I come to the interesting comments of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre who thinks that the simple procedure in regard to the grain handling system is to do nothing for five years, to have a five-year delay in the removal of branch lines, without regard to the fact that this is a matter of cost, and it is not just a cost to the rail system but a cost to the elevator system which is served by it which also is significantly higher than it need be if the grain is moved through fewer houses.
We have said repeatedly that in our view these facts relating to cost should be made clearly available to producers-we have been doing a great deal to ensure that this will happen-and the producers should have a chance to choose whether they receive the lower-cost system, with the changes which are required to bring it about, or whether they are willing to pay for the higher-cost system thus avoiding the adjustments which are involved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recently assured western Canada that it is the intention of his government to lend a more attentive ear to problems voiced by western Canadians. He maintained that the difficulties confronting western Canada concerned him and his government as much as did those of any other region of Canada. However, as one who feels he has some understanding of the situation in western Canada, I doubt the government's sincerity, and so do the people. Our scepticism can be attributed to numerous instances in the past where a succession of Liberal governments have failed to honour their commitments to the west. "Credibility" is the word. History has made it hard for us to be very optimistic.
No other single issue in recent years has damaged the government's credibility in Winnipeg and Manitoba as much as the transfer of the Air Canada overhaul base from Winnipeg to Dorval. This House is quite familiar with the circumstances, both past and present, surrounding the transfer. However, let me once again briefly acquaint the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) with the history of the transfer and some of the repercussions which have followed because of it.
To most Air Canada employees who were transferred from Winnipeg to Dorval, the year 1948 is synonymous with the appointment of G. R. McGregor as TCA president. In that year rumours started that the airline was moving out of Manitoba. McGregor, who was born and raised in Montreal, was instrumental in moving the headquarters' staff to Montreal. Over the years he achieved, as the records show, the relocation of most of the TCA operations that were originally started in Winnipeg. While the moves were actually taking place, Mr. McGregor and C. D. Howe, then the minister of transport, denied there was any transfer in progress. For example, in July, 1948, Mr. Howe said that 95 per cent of TCA would remain in Winnipeg. In July, 1949, Mr. McGregor stated:
TCA's long association with Winnipeg has been a very happy one, and will continue ... in Winnipeg.
He also said:
The cost of moving it would be tremendous and TCA would be moving from an area in which it can hire good mechanical help in an apparently abundant supply, to an area where that supply, both as quality and quantity, is not comparable.
This was the case, and still is. When TCA was established in 1937, Winnipeg was chosen as the overhaul centre by a group of unbiased American experts who based their choice on all the pertinent factors, that is, dry climate, clear flying weather, land values, construction costs, taxation, etc. Presumably, these experts had no axe to grind and were solely interested in locating in the most logical area of Canada. This they did. When the facilities were transferred outright in 1969, the base was an extremely efficient and well administered operation with the capacity to handle jet age aircraft and technology.
Transportation Policy
At any rate, the 1950s saw repeated denials by government officials of a wholesale transfer. Nevertheless, the transfer continued. For example, in 1951 the major portion of the engineer's department and a number of radio technicians were moved. The year 1952 saw the communications laboratory moved to Dorval. In March of 1963, Mr. Pearson stated that it was in the national interest that Winnipeg should be an air centre and TCA operations and services should continue to this end. Mr. Pearson also stated: "The proper location of TCA's facilities and services will be determined in a manner which is fair and equitable to the city of Winnipeg." In December of that year, Manitoba was assured by Mr. Pearson: " ... it is the policy of the government to do everything possible to maintain employment at the TCA base in Winnipeg, and if possible to increase it."
In a letter dated May 23, 1968, to Premier Weir of Manitoba, the Prime Minister wrote: "You may be assured that the present government will honour the commitment made by my predecessor, the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, and that we will, in addition, vigorously search out alternatives aimed at maintaining a viable aircraft support industry in Manitoba." These were merely a few of the promises made to the people of Winnipeg, employees of Air Canada and the aerospace industry in Manitoba. In the end, the Air Canada overhaul operation in Winnipeg was phased out. CAE Aircraft, a division of Northwest Industries of Edmonton, acquired the base and was assured of federal government assistance in establishing itself as a viable substitute for Air Canada in Winnipeg. The firm, however, has been beset with financial difficulties.
Skilled personnel have had to leave Manitoba and seek employment elsewhere. Former Air Canada employees who chose to stay in Winnipeg rather than move to Dorval have finally had to relocate there. Where is the federal government now? What about the promises to maintain a viable aircraft industry in the province? This is what I mean by the term "credibility" that I mentioned earlier. The federal government has none in Manitoba. There is only a credibility gap. The government has failed miserably thus far in honouring its promises.
Rather than cite a surfeit of other promises and agreements in which federal government officials assured us that the future of Air Canada in Winnipeg was secure, I would like to dwell on a vitally important factor which often has been overlooked in this entire fiasco. This is the human factor. For several months I have been studying the events and circumstances surrounding the transfer of this overhaul base to Dorval. I have received great quantities of mail from individuals who were transferred from Winnipeg to Dorval. I have travelled there and talked with the employees, and plan to do so soon again. From all of this I have learned of the tremendous costs being incurred by the operation at Dorval. It is neither efficient nor economical.
But beyond all this is the effect of such a move upon the Air Canada employee, upon the individual's well-being. Worker morale at Dorval is low. Many employees resent having been forced to move because of lack of employment in Winnipeg. They blame the government. Social

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
commentator Vance Packard points out in his book "A Nation of Strangers" that North Americans who are forced to move often encounter psychological problems which are more acute than people realize. Packard says that people who have no roots in the area to which they move often become isolated and indifferent to community problems, while being obsessed with their own difficulties. In studying aerospace communities, Packard discovered that their ever-changing populations are often beset by everything from infidelity to alcoholism. This book is an exhaustive study which attempts to alert people to the hazards of mobility. The problems Packard discusses obviously exist in many communities, and from what I know of the Dorval situation I would not be surprised to discover there pronounced difficulties of this nature.
It is time the government took heed of the situation. As Manitoba's representative in the cabinet, the Minister of National Defence must press for action. The people of Manitoba can no longer depend on the Prime Minister and his promises. It also appears that we can no longer cjepend upon the hon. member for Winnipeg South, either. Was it not he who said that the transfer was "one of the worst decisions made in Canadian history"? It was also he who said: "No one endorses more strongly than I do the concept of decentralization of industrial activity." Yet the minister is content to acquiesce while the government of which he is part does nothing to act upon its promises to the city of Winnipeg and to the aerospace industry in Manitoba. Instead, the government tries to bribe the people of Manitoba with token gestures announced by a Minister of National Defence whose credibility rating is quickly declining.
The Minister of National Defence has refused to inspect the Dorval situation, and to my knowledge-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one subject which has dominated Canadian parliaments ever since this country was put together, it must be the subject of transportation. If there is one thing this country is dependent upon, it is of course transportation. For that reason it has always been dominant in the speeches of parliamentarians and of people outside politics.
Transportation is the vital link which holds, or tries to hold, this country together. Successive governments have attempted to deal with it in order to come up with a policy that will satisfy all aspects of Canada. Of course, Mr. Speaker, this country being the kind of country it is, there

has never been a policy which has satisfied all parts of it; and listening to this debate and hearing hon. members from all sides, I must say I have not heard any policy tonight which will satisfy all parts of the country.
In particular, the speech given by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) who led off the debate was lacking in any ideas as to changes that might take place. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) was a little more constructive in that he had something to offer, even though he was going to settle the problem by nationalizing it all, thereby sweeping it under the rug, and taxing the Canadian people to provide services that are not necessarily economic, sensible or reasonable.
I come from an area of Canada which I call on the outer fringes. By that I mean it is not an area near or attached directly to any of the metropolitan centres of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Consequently, the problem that the people in my region face is very similar to that faced by those represented by the hon. member for Vegreville and by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, in that our areas have declining population vis-a-vis the metropolitan centres.
The argument, of course, is over whether or not this decline in population, this change in our economic fortunes has been caused by economic policies, by tariff policies, by transportation policies, or whatever. But the point, surely, is that in a dynamic country such as Canada, which is basically still a developing country, there cannot be any policy that is static, that is stable, to deal with a problem which is continually evolving. In other words, anybody who comes to the House of Commons and says, "I have the answer for now and forever" is making the assumption that the country is never going to change, and that of course is ridiculous.
What all this means is that any policies we propose and legislate, we must be prepared to overthrow in a few years as the country develops in ways which are unbeknownst to us. In an area such as northwestern Ontario, its problems are compounded by the fact that the federal government, looking at the over-all statistics as to how Canada operates, regards my area as part of the wealthiest province of all. When you want to talk about a problem that is of legitimate concern to the people of northwestern Ontario, the federal government says, "You must go to the government of Ontario because it has the power and, more important, the money that is necessary for dealing with the problem." In addition, of course, most of the province's population is not distributed around the northwest but is to be found in the golden horseshoe area, in and around Toronto. This means that our transportation problems are never considered as serious as those of eastern Ontario, simply because the population is not in our area. The population is in and around Toronto, not in the north. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, although we have a pretty good idea of what our transportation problems are, we can never find any way of obtaining substantial redress.
Let me indicate some of the frustrations the people of my area have experienced in the fields of national and provincial transportation policies. It seems to us that
March 20, 1973

those policies, hand in hand, discriminate against those who are isolated from the metropolitan centres. Whether this discrimination is deliberate or accidental, I cannot say. Nevertheless, it does happen, probably naturally, because both governments are inclined to pay more attention to the larger centres of population than to the more sparsely settled areas.
The size of the problem was brought home to me when the government announced in the Speech from the Throne that there would be a conference of western provinces to discuss transportation problems. By definition, Mr. Speaker, that eliminated the province of Ontario and eliminated my region which on most issues has more in common with the west than with the province of Ontario.

speechtext: Northwestern Ontario is the great land bridge between the Prairies and eastern centres such as Hamilton. Our problem is that transportation systems seem to be designed to pass through, around and over our area but not to stop there and participate in the growth of the area. This is frustrating because even though the area from which I come is in the centre of Canada, very little happens there. Whether this is because of transportation circumstances, the nature of the climate or the resources with which we deal, I do not know. However, our birth rate is high.

speechtext:
So we face a number of problems in dealing with transportation systems. Part of our problem is that often the needs of our area do not fit into the national pattern or even into the existing provincial pattern. Let me give Your Honour a brief example. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre berated TransAir for obtaining a franchise to run between Winnipeg and Toronto. The route goes from Winnipeg to Dryden, Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, Toronto and back. This franchise was granted so that Trans Air could serve northwestern Ontario adequately. Another service was to operate from Winnipeg to Thunder Bay and to Toronto. The idea was that this service would subsidize jet service to northwestern Ontario and throughout northern Manitoba.
Since there are no subsidies available for tertiary carriers of this nature, the Canadian Transport Commission provided those runs to permit TransAir to upgrade its equipment. When they first began their service throughout northwestern Ontario, they used DC3s. The route went from Winnipeg to Kenora, Dryden, Thunder Bay and Sault Ste. Marie along with another service that used a jet for servicing Winnipeg, Thunder Bay and Toronto. For awhile this was a perfectly acceptable solution. Then the traffic grew so much on the former route that Trans Air replaced the aircraft used with those of greater capacity; more traffic was generated from my section of northwestern Ontario than had been anticipated. Unfortunately, the increase in traffic encouraged Trans Air to put a jet on that service, which eliminated the town of Kenora from the direct service it had enjoyed. The existing service was replaced by one utilizing YS-11A aircraft. That
Transportation Policy
service has since degenerated and a twin-engine Otter aircraft is used.
Although the general transportation system of the area has been improved because of the jet service, made possible by providing Trans Air with a route with which to subsidize the former route, in towns like Kenora there has been a substantial deterioration of service resulting from the improved equipment which Trans Air is using. This, it strikes me, is one of the problems which all such small communities need to face.
As diesels have been introduced, and jet aircraft, the improved equipment can only operate effectively over longer distances, which means that communities lying in between must suffer a deterioration of service which can only be described as substantial. One has only to look at the way in which the railways now treat areas in between major centres. No longer do they have agents in these small communities and no longer do they maintain telegraph service there. Instead, they maintain service centres, which means that one must get in touch with the railway by long distance telephone to reach the appropriate office in one of the larger centres. Nothing except substantially diminishing service is available to the people of these small communities. For example, no longer is it possible at Dryden or Kenora for freight to be dropped off at the station. If a shipment is coming from Toronto, it must go to Winnipeg and be shipped back.

speechtext:
In talking about transportation we must ask, who is to pay? The difficulty we face is that the railways, airlines and other modes of transportation improve in efficiency, they do not improve the efficiency of service to smaller centres. Rather, they improve the efficiency of service to larger centres. This has put tremendous pressure on smaller communities which need to be served. Whether this has happened as a result of deliberate action on the part of those involved in the transportation system, or whether it is natural evolution of the kind which has taken place on the world market is a question open to debate and it is a point with which I do not intend to deal. What we are talking about is the provision of service to small communities. In any discussion of this nature concerning transportation, we must determine what is a fair and adequate rate structure, then determine who is to bear the extra cost, and then who must bear the cost of the subsidy.
I recall when I was a member of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications that we discussed the elimination of the "Dominion" train which at that time travelled across Canada. We met with both CPR and CNR officials. One statement attributed to the president of the CPR, at that time Mr. Sinclair, was to the effect that even if the "Dominion" train were operating at 100 per cent capacity, and even if a row of seats were to be put on top of the train, open to the elements, enough revenue would still not be generated to pay the expenses. We heard the same story from the CNR. At that time Canadian National
