speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I confess that I was somewhat disappointed in the opening remarks of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon when he, in true Pavlovian fashion, executed that old knee jerk reaction as he repeated once again the old refrain about the failure of public ownership in his province of Saskatchewan-failure due, alas, to that wicked NDP government. But he did recover somewhat, I thought, as he went on to castigate the failure of the present government to enunciate any kind of intelligible transportation policy.
Things picked up for the government, however, when the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) rose to speak. His eulogistic phrases for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) dropped like the gentle rain from heaven and I listened with rapt attention until he spoke so glowingly of the minister's Herculean efforts in the area of railroad pensions. At that point I shut off my speaker because I realized that the gentle rain had made him all wet. I am not going to attack the Minister of Transport. If anything, I would commiserate with him for he, poor soul, has inherited several generations of bungling from successive Tory and Liberal governments who would not know a transportation policy from a Prince Albert radish, whatever that is.
Canadian transportation policy started with John A. Macdonald who united this country with a band of steel, as the historians put it. Also, at the same time we gave away half of this country to the CPR, an act which gave that company an advantage which it has never yielded: it still owns a great part of Canada, one way or another. In the days of R. B. Bennett and Mackenzie King, the Canadian railway situation was pretty desperate. The

public investment in the CNR and CPR, not counting the CNR debts to the government on which no interest was paid, amounted to $2,200,000,000. Railway transportation was such a mess that CNR president Sir Henry Thornton suggested a royal commission to attack the whole problem. The commission was struck, and like most Tory and Grit commissions it achieved nothing but more expense to the taxpayer. Is anyone surprised?
At the time there was a suggestion that the two railways be merged under public ownership, but the commission opposed that idea. So did the other place. In fact, a group of Montreal bankers, throwing up their hands in shocked horror, made a counter proposal that the CPR take over the CNR in the interests of private entrepreneurship. But, fortunately, the Canadian people would have none of it since the majority believed in public ownership. Various other measures were suggested and some tried, but nothing worked, and by 1937 the Canadian people were paying interest charges on a debt of $3 billion, a debt which became a millstone around the necks of the Canadian people.
In 1973 we still have a national railway and a private railway, with the private company still skimming off the goodies and the national railway running a poor second. The Canadian people have long since accepted the principle of public ownership of railways. All that remains, Mr. Speaker, is to persuade the representatives of the people that it is in the best interests of Canada to take over the CPR and to develop one unified transportation system whose main function would be to provide fast, safe and efficient service for the people of Canada.
This brings me to the next matter that I wish to speak of in connection with railways. I would like to speak of the inequities that plague the men and women who work for our own national railway system, the CNR. When referring to the CPR, just multiply by two. One would think that since the CNR is wholly-owned by the people of Canada, it would be concerned to provide much needed jobs at a time when unemployment is one of the social problems of greatest concern to its owners, the Canadian public. In actual fact, according to the information I have, the CNR is busily engaged in reducing the size of its work force on the west coast, is showing a lamentable lack of interest in providing necessary safety precautions in the Fraser canyon, and is doing its best to compete with the CPR in providing the worst possible pension scheme.
Hardly a day goes by that I and my colleagues do not receive letters and phone calls from disgruntled railroad employees. The present work-to-rule situation is only symptomatic of poor working conditions that have accumulated over the years to the point at which major concessions will have to be made to head off widespread disruption of essential rail services. In British Columbia, one of the chief complaints is that CNR yardmen in the greater Vancouver terminal are being forced to reduce switch crews from three men to two men. This reduction is all perfectly legal since the workingmen found themselves in a position of having to sign an agreement or else go to arbitration. Since the box score for arbitration has been nine to one for the employers, there did not seem much point in opposing the arbitration. Already 13 crews have been reduced and 25 more are scheduled to be
March 20, 1973

reduced in the next 11 months. Crews have been reduced in Edmonton as well. And this at a time when the entire nation is concerned about unemployment.
I am a shareholder in the CNR in the same sense that every Canadian citizen is a shareholder. It disturbs me to hear that the CNR is reducing crews at the risk of reducing safety, that longer and longer trains are being coupled, that niggardly pensions are reluctantly granted, all in the name of productivity. Railroad engineers are deeply concerned about hazardous conditions in the Fraser canyon. They speak of the absence of ditch lights and slide fences that have not been reset for a considerable time. They tell of an engineer stuck in a snowslide for just short of 38 hours with no food and no apparent attempt to get it to him, and of another engineer on snow plow duty for over 23 hours without rest or eating facilities.
All of this, Mr. Speaker, is intended to reinforce the point that in the formulation of a national transportation policy, in the operation of a publicly-owned railroad, the prime factors to be considered should be safety and service-safety not only for the men who have got to make their living railroading, but also for the public which depends on these facilities.
The reputation of our railroads for poor treatment of its employees is shameful. The hon. member for Prince Albert has already made reference to the poor morale on our national railway. I will not dwell on the pension aspect at this time because this is a subject that has been brought up in this chamber time and time again and will continue to be brought up until a decent pension allowance is made to men who have given their lives in the service of the people of Canada. I would hope that in the negotiations now under way there will be better treatment of railway employees, because whether we are speaking of an army or an army of workers they will not be effective unless consideration is given to the important question of morale.
Related to the topic of rail transport is the proposal by Premier Barrett to utilize existing railroading trackage for the transport of oil from Alaska through the Yukon and British Columbia and by pipeline to Seattle. On the face of it, his proposal seems eminently sensible. All that would be needed in terms of railroad construction would be a relatively short extension of the Alaska railroad to connect with the B.C. railroad at Lower Post.
Setting aside the economic implications for the moment, one salient point emerges, namely, that this route is the most acceptable one from a "people standpoint". The transport of oil by tanker off the shores of British Columbia has met with continuous opposition from people on both sides of the border and will continue to meet with opposition. How anyone can seriously defend such a route escapes me. When we realize that 70 per cent of the earth's surface consists of ocean, and when we reflect on the disturbing trend to build larger and larger tankers-we are threatened with tankers approaching
500,000	tons in size-we must surely realize that we are ultimately faced with the problem of oceans being incapable of sustaining marine life.
Transportation Policy
Pipelines such as the proposed Mackenzie valley pipeline threaten to create similar environmental havoc and such proposals are being opposed almost as strenuously as the use of tankers. We hear reports that the people of the north will simply not allow the pipeline to be built; that they will blow it up if necessary. I have never heard any objection expressed to the transportation of oil by railroad. In fact, the concept seems to satisfy people generally as an alternative choice to both sea transport and to pipeline transport. The difficulty seems to be that the decision-makers think in economic terms mainly, while the people most affected think in terms of the effect on their surroundings, on the quality of life in Canada's future.
I do not pretend to be an expert on the transportation of oil or on the building of railways, and for this I make no apology. We all have our areas of competency. Mine lay in the teaching field. Some hon. members on my right are experts on points of order that are not points of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
But what interests me in this question of alternative oil routes is the reaction of the government, as expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), to the proposal of Mr. Barrett. When the plan first became public, the Prime Minister did not indicate approval; the Prime Minister did not indicate disapproval of the plan, but he did manage to indicate by an enthusiastic lack of enthusiasm a completely negative approach to the plan even before details of it were known to members of the House.
I would not for a moment suggest without further study, that this plan is preferable to others, but I do suggest most strenuously that it should be given extremely serious consideration by the government and by all members of the House, as should any plan to transport oil by rail rather than by pipeline through permafrost, or by ship through our oceans. We are not concerned here solely with the economic feasibility of an oil route. We should not be concerned with political gamesmanship.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Heavens, no!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: We should not descend to consideration of whether the reigning provincial oil route critic has been included in negotiations or not. We should be concerned mainly with the welfare of future generations and the environment in which we will live. It is this principle that should govern consideration of a national transportation policy, whether of people, goods or oil.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles E. Haliburton (South Western Nova):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH A NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise as a member from a rural riding in the maritime provinces and I trust the House will bear with me if I seem to typify some of the opinions held in that area. In a rural riding we have greater distances to travel than perhaps other Canadians in order to get to various facilities. We have greater distances to ship our goods. One might well assume that in those circumstances the greater distances involved would result in cheaper transportation rates per mile for the carriage of our goods and
26087-8)

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
for the carriage of our people. Instead of having a cheaper mileage rate of such transportation, we in fact pay a higher rate. Instead of getting a break on rates we are, in a sense, kicked by them. It actually costs more per mile to ship goods in the maritime provinces than it does in the wealthier parts of Canada. In fact, it costs 50 per cent more, Mr. Speaker, to travel on the railroad in Nova Scotia than it does to travel between Montreal and Toronto. I am sure you will agree that that is not the way to remove disparities among provinces.
Rural Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a frontier. It begs to be developed. Atlantic Canada is largely rural, and it begs to be developed. Railways were originally considered an instrument of development in this country but they have defaulted in that function. British Columbia Rail, or B.C. Rail as it is called, is an instrument of development in British Columbia and it is performing a fantastic operation there. Go-go transit in Ontario is another illustration of how development can be put into effect by the railways.
Now even the province of New Brunswick is getting into the act with a scheme which I suppose will be called N.B. Rail. They are going to take over the railroad in order to help develop that province. But the fact that these several provinces are getting into the railroad business is indicative of the bankruptcy of the policy of the government which has been in power for so many years in Canada. It is indicative of the bankruptcy of policy to the extent that transportation in this country, which is supposed to be a national responsibility, is being taken over by the provinces.
I was encouraged by the announcement of the minister on December 18 that a northwest transportation plan was being considered. I hope it comes to fruition. But I would earnestly recommend to the minister that he consider not only that great frontier of northern Canada for development by means of better rail transportation, but also the frontier which is epitomized by the Atlantic provinces, a frontier which has yet to be developed. It is an area which should certainly share in the development which will one day be Canada. I express the hope that greater federal and provincial co-operation, as was envisaged in the announcement of the minister in December, can become a reality in the rest of Canada and that such a spirit of development can be applied with regard to Nova Scotia.
Not only should the theory of development be applied in the case of railways, Mr. Speaker; it should also be applied with regard to ferry services. Ferry services are a problem very close to the hearts of those in western Nova Scotia whom I represent. What is the history of the ferry service in western Nova Scotia? It is evidence of the typical lack of concern which has been shown by federal authorities for transportation in that area. We do have two Canadian ferries running across the Bay of Fundy, one of which is owned by the CPR and has, thank goodness, been upgraded in the past few years and provides a fairly efficient service, albeit at a little more expense than the local people feel should be necessary if industry is to be encouraged in the area. However, I am not going to dwell on that ferry. I want to mention in some detail the ferry which runs between Yarmouth and Bar Harbour. That ferry, the Bluenose is now 17 years old. It was built at a

time when trucks were a good deal shorter and when trains were a good deal longer. It was built to accommodate traffic of the 1950s and it is no longer adequate to accommodate the traffic of the 1970s.
According to a report appearing in our provincial daily on January 24, senior officials of the Department of Transport, senior officials of the CNR and senior officials of the provincial government were to meet to discuss the possible replacement of that ferry. That news report indicated that the provincial officials expected that after the meeting they would have some concrete answers in approximately two weeks. Well, that was some six weeks ago now and there has been no answer. Although I have diligently sought information from the department in the meantime, I have not been able to ascertain what the future holds in store for this ferry. The only answer I have been able to get is that perhaps a survey will be undertaken.
May I remind the minister, who was not in his present portfolio a few years ago, that in 1967-68 a competent firm, A. D. Margison and Associates, did a study in depth of the type of vessel that ought to be used on that service from the point of view of potential traffic. I suggest it would take only a very short time to update that study and to design the type of ferry that is necessary. In addition, one factor that Margison did not get any input on in their study is that a couple of foreign ferries are plying the waters between Yarmouth and the New England shore. One of them has been operating for a couple of years with very great success, and I suggest a lesson is to be learned from the success of that operation. It is most regrettable that Canadian entrepreneurs or the Canadian government did not have sufficient fortitude to place a vessel on that service long before it became necessary for the traffic to be taken up by a foreign owner.
I have been speaking of the necessity of transportation development and I now want to say a word about industry in the maritime provinces and particularly in my area. I represent an area which is largely a small business area. Very few of these businesses are able to grow into big businesses in the terms we think of big businesses in central Canada. You may ask Mr. Speaker, why that is. Why is it that living standards and incomes in our area tend to be lower than they are in other areas of Canada? Why is it that our successful businesses fail to grow into big businesses? Is it because we are less intelligent as a people than Upper Canadians? Enough maritimers have left their mark on Canadian universities to refute that idea. Are we less ambitious than Upper Canadians? Enough maritimers have achieved success in business in Upper Canada to refute that suggestion. Are we less in tune with the flow of events than Upper Canadians, or are we less shrewd? The Maritimes has produced more prime ministers and perhaps more ministers of finance than any other area in Canada, which I suggest refutes that argument.
So why is it, Mr. Speaker, that we appear to be a little backward? Why is it that even in the cradle of confederation itself the structures of this country are questioned? I suggest to you that, more than any other reason, the answer simply is: transportation. What does it do to us?
March 20, 1973

What does it do to the small businessman in my constituency? I can give the House some hint. If anybody in my constituency wants to go into the canning business, it will cost him at least two cents more per can to get his products on the shelves of stores owing to the cost of transportation of his cans.
Let me take another example, the fruit business. It cost about $1 per case to get apples to the major markets of Canada, which is enough to wipe out all the profit that is possible, and then some. Potatoes, apples, processed fruits and vegetables, fish products all face that same high tariff; I suggest it cannot be described as anything else. Transportation costs constitute a tariff on our goods entering the great Canadian market.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who is only just getting adjusted to his new portfolio, and very enthusiastically according to his parliamentary secretary, has a great opportunity in his present position to remove a great deal of the disparity in transportation costs in Canada. He has the benefit of his experience gained with DREE in his previous portfolio and he must know the difficulty of attempting to get industry to locate in the maritime provinces, in the west, in eastern Quebec, even in parts of Ontario, largely because of transportation costs. The experience that this minister has derived from DREE, coupled with his new knowledge and enthusiasm in regard to transportation matters, can serve the government in good stead if he will formulate a transportation policy that will assist in solving, rather than perpetuating, the disparities that exist between the have and the have-not regions of this country.
Hon. members may say of the transportation difficulties in the Maritimes, "Ah ha, but you have the advantage in regard to export markets; you do not have to send your products to central Canada". But even here the transportation policies of the major companies play tricks on you. It costs more to send a containerload of apples from Kentville, in the Annapolis valley, to Europe than it does from Hamilton, Ontario. Similarly, it costs more to ship grain from Saskatchewan to Nova Scotia than it does to ship it from Saskatchewan to northern Europe. In those circumstances it is very difficult indeed for the people in our area to compete effectively.
We have a misconception about transportation facilities in Canada, and indeed in North America. We take the approach that transportation facilities should be profitmaking enterprises. Why is this so? After all, we do not believe that the streets in our cities should make a profit; these are a necessary part of infrastructure, a necessary means of commerce. We do not believe that our highways should make a profit, even though there are substantial licensing fees, gas taxes, and so on. So why is it that in North America transportation facilities, which are vital in binding the country together and in enabling people in one area to compete effectively with people in another area, should be required to show a profit?
I suggest it is high time that this House and the government recognized that the Canadian transportation system, particularly the railways, is not and should not be thought of as a profit making endeavour only, or even primarily. The primary purpose of railways in Canada is that which was conceived in 1867 by Sir John A. Macdonald and the
Transportation Policy
Fathers of Confederation: the railways are an instrument of development. They should be an instrument of unity, an instrument to remove regional disparities in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while other industries in this country show really aggressive approaches, in my opinion the railroads are very, very backward. Situated as I am in mid-Canada, in the area of Thunder Bay, one of Canada's largest harbours, a harbour that on a monthly basis when it is open carries the greatest tonnage of any harbour in Canada-

speechtext:
The same speech, and the same railroads too. Situated in the middle of this country, I see the role of the railroads as linking one part of the country with the other part. Yet I see a railroad system that is very weak and unaggressive, one that does not take opportunities when opportunities come along. In many ways the two railroads of this country do not want to run a railroad. I mention their approach to the provision of passenger service as an example. In my area recently 22 operators and other workers were laid off by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
So-called service centres have now been established in most of the places along the route, but they are a disgrace if the one that we found in the old city of Port Arthur is anything to go by, with plaster hanging off the ceiling, and so on. Because the agencies are no longer there, the service falls off and people are not able to buy tickets at the station. A sign on the door tells them to get their ticket at a travel agency. A year or two from now, Mr. Speaker, the CPR will come back to the public asking for larger subsidies because they are losing money, and it is because of the kind of non-aggressive approach that they are taking now.
Where were the railways when the issue of the Pickering airport first arose? Did they present a ground alternative; did they propose rapid ground transportation? No, they were not to be seen. Last week the Premier of British Columbia introduced the idea of a railroad alternative to the Mackenzie valley pipeline. At about the same time I was speaking in the committee on Indian affairs and northern development about the same kind of matter, only I was speaking of a rail pipeline along the east side of the Rockies.
A group working at Queen's University, called the Canadian Institute of Guided Ground Transport, has made some studies on this approach. They suggested that a railroad is a viable alternative to this particular pipeline. The difficulty with the pipeline is that it requires that the oil carried be heated to 150 degrees to 180 degrees in order to move in the Arctic, and therefore a pipeline cannot safely be burried in the ground because it would melt the permafrost.
This group at Quenn's University was lightly funded by the government and given some meagre support by the CNR and other groups. It maintains that 20 trains can move the same amount of oil per day as a 48-inch pipeline, that is, two million barrels. It is commonly accepted today

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
that the pipeline route would cost $5.3 billion. A railroad, on the other hand, could be built for about $2.5 billion, according to this study. The operating cost for the pipeline, including amortization of the $5.3 billion at roughly 8 per cent, would amount to $425 million per year. It is estimated that the operating cost of the railroad would be in the neighbourhood of $400 million per year-it would be higher except for the saving in the amortization cost.
This group has indicated several advantages of the railroad. The first is that the railroad is expandable. Their figures are based on a two-track system and they maintain that a one-track system would carry the 20 trains a day. Secondly, the railroad could carry liquefied gas, minerals, etc., as well as oil. Thirdly, the railroad could go both ways, taking people and goods in both directions. And fourthly, the railroad would employ more people on an annual basis: 4800 is the figure used in the study. Another factor which must be considered, if these figures are correct, is the lower investment which of course could have some meaning in the long-term relative to our monetary position with the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I bring up three points to show that the railroads are not aggressive. First, the passenger service which is deteriorating; second, the failure to look at fast ground transportation; third, the failure of the railroads to take a stand and do something about the Mackenzie valley pipeline alternative. The figures that were given at the committee the other night would seem to indicate that the amount of money spent on the Mackenzie valley pipeline study was in the neighbourhood of $40 million and the amount spent on the railroad study was a paltry $80,000. Something has to be done, Mr. Speaker, and the government can help by putting more money into this suggested alternative. However, the railroads in this country must take a stronger position, become more responsive to the needs of the modern Canadian community and develop a far more aggressive stance to problems of the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should deal briefly with the history of the problem in southwestern Ontario. On October 1, 1970, there was a decision referred to by Southam News Service as "the land mark decision". The Canadian Transport Commission allowed the discontinuation of railway passenger service on 400 miles of track in southwestern Ontario, involving six train lines. The decision followed extensive public hearings held in Owen Sound and Guelph at which more than 70 people presented briefs. Included among these were federal and provincial members of parliament and representatives of municipal councils.
With us tonight, Mr. Speaker, we have the reeve of Elora. Either he or his representative made recommendations at that hearing. There were representatives of other public groups and private individuals who were concerned about this matter. There were representatives from councils for the province of Ontario and from a number of other provinces. Without exception, every brief presented at these hearings, except for the briefs of the railway companies, were in opposition to the discontinuance of those railway lines.
Nevertheless, the Canadian Transport Commission ruled, setting a precedent, that these lines could be allowed to be discontinued. On April 6, 1971, my predecessor, Mr. Howe, moved a motion to the effect that the Commons committee on transport and communications hold public hearings in the affected areas of southwestern Ontario. This motion was passed by the committee despite the fact that the Liberals on the committee, with the exception of the hon. member for London, voted to block the hearings taking place. Hearings were held late last spring in southwestern Ontario, at several centres. There were 55 briefs presented and 68 witnesses heard. I should like to read briefly the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications:
Therefore your committee recommends that all rail passenger services which were discontinued on November 1, 1970, should be re-established immediately and a moratorium should be placed on all pending passenger train discontinuance applications in Canada, until the study referred to hereafter is completed, as recommended in many briefs and particularly in that brief presented by the government of the province of Ontario.
Beyond that, it recommends that immediately a tri-level study be undertaken to discuss the totality of the problem in Canada to make sure that proper service is provided
March 20,1973

for all Canadians. That was a committee dominated by the Liberal party. It had a Liberal majority; it had a Liberal chairman and a Liberal co-chairman. The report of the committee came in. It was presented to the government. The government has refused to act on it since that time.
In reply to questions in respect of this service, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has adamantly refused to do anything until he has had consultations with the government of the province of Ontario, despite the fact that the federal government has sole responsibility for passenger services in this country, and despite the fact that the province of Ontario is on record on two occasions, before the Canadian Transport Commission and also before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, as favouring the immediate reinstatement of these railway services.
The minister referred, in supporting his case, to what he erroneously called the Soberland report, which was a study commissioned by the CTC and carried out by Dr. Soberman, on commuter rail services for metropolitan Toronto. The minister seems to feel that nothing could be done in respect of acceptance or rejection of this report until such time as he spoke to the province of Ontario regarding these rail services which are commuter services around Toronto.
This has absolutely nothing to do with the problem of discontinuance of service on those six rail lines in Ontario. If the minister had done his homework, he would be aware of this. The delay is unconscionable. The government knew it had a majority on the committee. Government members supported the report as well as our members. All the local representatives, the local members of parliament, the local members of the provincial parliament who were present, the members of citizens' groups and the members of local municipalities who spoke, were in support of the reinstatement of this service. There is no question about it. There is nothing to study before the minister brings back the service. We need action on this right now.
Today we were asked by members on the other side to be constructive in our criticism. They felt that perhaps we had not been constructive. I say my constructive criticism is that if they seriously want to improve the rail service, they could get to work and accept the report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I can promise hon. members opposite that if the government refuses to act, a progressive Conservative government will get those trains moving again.
Let me speak briefly about the question of whether the railways have attempted in good faith to provide adequate service for the people of southwestern Ontario. I think one newspaper article from the London Free Press of Saturday January 5, 1973, illustrates very well the sort of service they have been providing. It goes like this:
Like most three-year-old boys, Teddy Evans of London loves trains.
So, on Nov. 17, his mother, Mrs. Edward R. (Donna) Evans of 52 Wellesley Cres., took him for his first train ride.
It wasn't exactly the kind of ride Mrs. Evans was expecting.
They boarded a Canadian National Railways train in London for Toronto where they were to meet Mr. Evans. She and her son
Transportation Policy
ended up in the baggage car with about 30 other passengers because the regular coaches were filled.
They had to sit on suitcases in the dimly-lit rough car amid baggage and other freight.
Mrs. Evans and some other passengers were startled when a body in a casket was put into the baggage car at Brantford.
"When they put the corpse on, that was a bit much," Mrs. Evans said.
The only window was in the door. It was "very dark and not meant for people to travel on," she said.
"CN didn't even apologize for putting the passengers in the baggage car," Mrs. Evans said.
"The conductor made a joke about it. He said "it's not everyone who can ride in the baggage car". The woman said: "What really bugged me was a newspaper article saying that train service is adequate but there aren't enough people to ride the trains."
Mrs. Evans said it was the first time she had travelled in a baggage car, and "I hope it's the last time."
Her son, Teddy, enjoyed the ride because it was his first time on a train, Mrs. Evans said.
"He was kind of upset because he couldn't see out."
The reporter was unable to get a comment from the passenger riding in the casket. Mr. Speaker, I can deal briefly with the CTC. The CTC asks whether uneconomic lines should be allowed to continue. This is how they define it:
To include such considerations as the cost of alternative modes of transportation as determinants of "uneconomic" would raise the possibility that highly unprofitable lines could be designated "economic" and therefore ineligible for subisdy only because alternative transportation is either unavailable or more costly. Such a result would be contrary to the national transportation policy-
I was interested to read, also, a quotation from the words of the Minister of Transport when he was president of the Confederation of National Trade Unions in 1961. He said that a transportation policy is closely tied to economic planning, and as such must be linked to the common good and not to the profitability of private enterprise. I hope he continues to think along those lines and gives us some action on this particular situation.
Surely, when the CTC makes these decisions it should take into consideration the cost of pollution in respect of driving people off the trains and into private automobiles, the rights of senior citizens and the rights of people who do not drive, the cost of alternative transportation which must be provided by the provinces, and the effect, most importantly, upon the development of the small communities of rural Canada which count upon decent transportation for their health.
Mr. Speaker, this government has shown a concern for the problems of regional disparity. I am asking tonight that it indicate that it is also concerned about rural Canadians in Ontario. A decent system of transportation is the right of all Canadians. The government could act tonight, show it has good faith and that it respects that right of all citizens in Canada to have the quality of life which they deserve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that this discussion has taken place. I am pleased, also that the Conservative party, particularly the last speaker, has indicated that it would make transportation work. When we speak of transportation we usually speak of railways. That is what the hon. member was speaking of. If it is to wprk, obviously some members of the Conser-

March 20, 1973
Transportation Policy
vative Party are of the opinion that we must renationalize the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, because there does not appear to be any other way in which we will get any action on the problem.
The hon. member did not mention that among our studies there are studies which have been done in other areas. We find in northern Ontario also that the Canadian Transport Commission has failed to provide an alternative to subsidy, and we find in the mid-Canada passenger train service that $10 million has been authorized to allow the companies to operate at a loss. Under the policy of the Canadian Transport Commission the railways are subsidized to the tune of 80 per cent. The railways immediately took most of their passenger lines, placed them in an uneconomical position and then asked the government to subsidize them.
The Russians, when they came to Canada on a number of occasions with committees of parliamentarians, indicated that they thought what we were developing better than anyone else was our transportation system. That is high praise, coming from people from a country which can put a Sputnik into space, travel around the moon and land on the moon. They can look at the Canadian transportation facilities and call them good. Obviously, we in this country have created a Canadian Transport Commission which is like the Senate and, like the Senate, I am prepared to abolish it now or at any other time.
We have retired Mr. Pickersgill so he can write his memoirs. I am surprised that with the facilities he had at the CTC he did not write those memoirs while he was the commissioner. Obviously, he did not. Now we have appointed Mr. Benson, a former minister of this government. I thought he would be there for a while, in as ineffective a position as was Mr. Pickersgill, because if I remember correctly Mr. Pickersgill had a certain facility, if nothing else, and a certain versatility of mind which enabled him to solve the machinations of Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway when he set his mind to it. I was surprised to hear that Mr. Benson is thinking of retiring.
Obviously, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) is waiting for a call to that place, as was made evident in the eulogy he delivered to his minister. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) must have been embarrassed on a number of occasions in the House, but I think it is safe to say he was embarrassed today and I feel sorry for anyone who has to take that kind of praise while he is still among the living, or certainly in an active position. Obviously, the minister will not be able to live up to the eulogy and for that reason I feel sorry for him.
Some suggestions have been made today, but I think most of them hinge on whether or not the government really wants to improve transportation in Canada. We have a facility which in my opinion can be modernized and made fit for the twentieth century. At present we are operating with broken down equipment, we are operating a major grain trade with cars which the government had to buy and then lend to the railway. I was interested to hear the prairie representative of the Liberal party trying to justify his relationship to the grain trade. He told us

that the government will offer a two-price system, one to the people who will accept the big elevators and hopper cars and the other to the other segment of the industry if they do not take advantage of his suggestions.
The whole industry is archaic. Railway transportation in Canada should not be archaic. Transportation by rail is surely the most efficient way of moving many of our basic commodities in this country. You cannot move them under a horse and buggy railroad system, yet that is the kind of system under which we operate. The prairie minister also mentioned that we cannot get rid of the debt of the CNR. Does he not realize that one cannot operate a national railway efficiently if there is a debt on that railway which has existed from the day it was started? We have done nothing since then but pay interest on that debt.
Surely he can see in that situation the same kind of burden as we have when we go to war. We now have a war to develop a transportation facility in this country that will be efficient. If that is so, surely we can add that debt to the rest of the national debt and allow the railway to operate without it. We should look at the tariff structure of the CNR and take away from the CPR that gravy train which they have had for so long at the expense of the Canadian people. If this minister wants to do nothing else, he can make some decision about what we are going to do with the debt of the CNR. Even if he does nothing else, he will have done something for transportation facilities in this country.
It is my opinion, and I think the opinion of many people-certainly one of the last speakers on the Liberal benches indicated that he had done some thinking about rail transportation into the high Arctic, both the east and west regions of the Arctic-that transportation by railway will have a role to play in the north. I agree with my colleague who said that we must be a bunch of idiots to spend the amount of money we are spending on STOL aircraft so that we can fly passengers from Ottawa to Montreal. The ground transportation facility that we have takes twice as long as the flight by air. It seems to me that unless you want to go for a ride, which you can do by going to any private airfield and paying five bucks for which they will take you up for a little look around, there is much better transportation by rail. This minister had better take a look at it, because if he does not I am afraid the Conservatives will not either.
However, I am also concerned that one of these days the Canadian public will take a look at this situation and will tell this government to supply that kind of transportation at a cost which they can pay. They will tell them to get rid of many of the problems which we are facing today in transportation. I suggest that one of the first things we should do is to take back the responsibility which parliament has for the national transportation policy of this nation, to take it away from the new Senate we have created, cease the political appointments that are made to that retirement body and again operate from this House a transportation policy for this nation and find solutions to some of our problems.
This is a very important motion. I think the Conservatives should be given credit for having stolen it from some of my colleagues, I am told, and also for at least bringing
March 20,1973

it forth because it is by far the best motion they have brought forth for some time. I think it would be profitable for the government to consider it and to do something about it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank hon. members for giving me a hand, but I hope they do not feel they have to stay because I see here the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Breau) who comes from New Brunswick and I know I shall get a very good hearing.
On March 12 I asked a question of the minister with respect to the shipbuilding subsidy program which runs out on March 31. I asked whether in view of the new planned oil refineries in the east the minister would give consideration to an extension of the shipbuilding subsidy beyond that date. The minister gave a reply that was thought to be optimistic. I am not trying to crowd in on the credit, if there is going to be an extension, but I want to put one or two facts on the record about this subsidy.
There is an interesting history to aid to shipbuilding in our country. It has been an ad hoc type of assistance throughout the years. It started in 1947, in the post-World War II period when the Canadian Maritime Commission was set up. As its major responsibility it had the development of a merchant marine and of a shipbuilding and ship repair industry commensurate with Canadian needs. As everyone knows, this move was not very successful.
In 1949, the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act was passed. This provided a fast write-off for owners of ships built in Canada and it had a reasonable amount of success. Then in 1964 the Canada Shipping Act was amended, and hon. members know some of the results of that. It did bring a few vessels under Canadian registration. In 1970 we had the shipbuilding temporary assistance program called STAP. It was brought in by the former minister and it has been reasonably successful. For example, the shipbuilding yard in Saint John, in which I am particularly interested, was able to obtain an order for three 30,000-ton tankers for export, which even though they are now of foreign country registration are being used on our east coast. This was quite profitable in
Adjournment Debate
terms of employment and enabled the yard to finish ahead in business. The subsidy was 17 per cent. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I should call it assistance rather than a subsidy. As I say it was 17 per cent, with a graduated downward formula.
The significant thing is that there has been a delay in the announcement of this program, and shipyards like to make their plans ahead of time. As I understand it, the international situation is still ripe for orders. The Canadian shipyards are well geared for work. They are reasonably efficient and they could fill some international orders. The companies, and the Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association, met with the minister and were given reason for some optimism. They are now asking for 20 per cent assistance on this occasion and they feel that the present is the proper time to make the move. The shipbuilding industry has not levelled off. It is on the downgrade since completing previous orders. Assistance given now would enable the shipyards to plan for the future, to keep up the different trades and it would also provide a future both for domestic and export orders.
I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is in the chamber, and I know he will be optimistic in his response. I hope he will take this chance to say that the government is really behind the industry for the first time in many years. The previous minister did make some moves and I gave him credit at the time. I know that the new minister is looking for opportunities such as this to help restore his tarnished image with respect to the auto pact.
This is an opportunity for the government to indicate that it is going to do something about an industry that is very important to us in the maritime provinces from an employment standpoint. I know the parliamentary secretary is going to create optimism about this matter. He is almost going to say that it will be acceptable. I hope he will go for the 20 per cent, really be enthusiastic and help his minister by giving us confidence for the future of this industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to answer my hon. friend for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell). I hope that I will not let him down. I am happy to see that he supports the Shipbuilding Temporary Assistance Program. It is a very good program, brought about, as he says, by a Liberal government.
He talked about the auto pact; I should like to assure him that, like the auto pact, STAP has been successful, even more successful in relative terms. As a matter of fact, it has helped in the export of ships from Canada to the order of $274 million. This represents 24 ships which have been built in several shipyards. I should mention that these ships are built in shipyards mainly in regions that need growth and employment, such as Sorel, Lauzon, Saint John and Halifax. We think it has been a very successful program. It has helped shipyards to modernize their facilities. It has helped them to become aware of export opportunities and to become competent from the marketing point of view. We think this will be good for the future.

March 20, 1973
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member has mentioned that the shipbuilding industry is concerned. We agree, and I hope that the government will deal expeditiously with this question because of that concern. As the hon. member knows, the date for application for assistance is March 31. The delivery date is October 31, 1975, which means that the shipbuilding industry can apply before March 31. I agree that we need a response, but there is no urgency because they have applied. They have made plans and will have work with respect to all the applications made before March 31, 1973.
I agree with the hon. member that it is a good program. There is no way that we can cut him down, because he promised this in his campaign and we are so happy to see that in his campaign he talked about good Liberal things. That is how he came to be elected so easily. We will try to continue that, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I see the parliamentary secretary is present and willing to give a positive response to my question tonight regarding greater utilization of the port of Churchill. I first asked on January 11 whether the government was to utilize further the port of Churchill and the minister at that time said in essence that he was studying the proposition. A couple of weeks later I asked the question again and the minister again said that he was studying the proposition. I think that has been the answer of ministers for the last 10, 20 or 30 years on the question of the utilization of the port of Churchill which is so important to us in western Canada.
We in the west have for long said that we have been discriminated against in many ways, basically because of the transport system and the freight rate structure in our country. One of the deals made when western Canada came into confederation was that we would supply the eastern industrial market with a cheap source of raw materials and that these would be the source of finished, manufactured goods which would come from eastern Canada. As a result, today in the west we find that there is still a great deal of unfairness in the freight rate structure, inasmuch as it is more expensive to ship a product from western Canada to the east than from eastern Canada to the west. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we were to better utilize the port of Churchill we could perhaps equalize some of the unfairness that exists in transportation systems that affect western Canadians. I believe that the port should be utilized much more than it is today.
Consider the city of Yorkton, from which I come. There is a plant there which builds houses. They ship these prefabricated houses to within 200 miles of the port of Churchill, which may mean that they send them 700, 800 or 900 miles from the city of Yorkton. But they do not ship the houses to Churchill by rail and put them on a barge. Instead, they ship them to Montreal, put them on a boat, take them down the St. Lawrence Seaway, around by Newfoundland and through Hudson Bay to their destination which is only a few hundred miles from the port of Churchill. I am told it is about four or five times as far as it would be if they were to ship these prefabricated-homes

from Yorkton to the port of Churchill and by barge to the destination, whether it is Rankin Inlet or Hudson Bay.
Why do they ship them that way when it is four or five times longer? It is for a simple reason. They do not have the facilities to handle prefabricated homes at the port of Churchill. They do not have any barges. In fact, they carry the prefabricated homes from the port of Churchill to the Indian or Eskimo settlements at Hudson Bay. That points out how stupid our transportation facilities are regarding the port of Churchill, and why the government must stop studying and start acting in order to build needed facilities at the port. There should be worthwhile facilities so that we in western Canada have the inland seaport we deserve.
The provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan are putting pressure on the federal government to act. Last summer there was a study by the premiers of those two provinces. They have now formed a group called the Port of Churchill Board to put pressure on the federal government and other powers that be. The port is closer to Europe, in terms of shipping our grain, by 1,100 miles than if we ship our grain through the Great Lakes, through Montreal and on to Europe. It is about 1,100 miles shorter than going down the St. Lawrence Seaway. I am told that for the farmer this would mean 10 cents to 16 cents a bushel that he would save on his wheat if it were shipped through the port of Churchill, but is not being done in significant volume today.
In 1944, about three million bushels of grain were shipped through the port of Churchill. In 1972, only 25 million bushels of grain were shipped through the port of Churchill, despite the fact we have the technology available that could improve the port at this time. I am told that this year only about half as much grain will be shipped through that port as there was in 1972.1 suggest it is time for action to improve the port.
I want to make one more point. The Hudson Bay Route Association has made many splendid recommendations over the years about this port. I think it should be commended for some of the work it has been done in drawing public attention to the reasons why we should increase the facilities there. I wish to read some of the recommendations they made in a letter they sent out in January 1973. They say that some of the following must be done:
1.	Deepening of the harbour next to the wharf
2.	Deepening of the "turn-around" basin
3.	Grain galleries to be lengthened and modernized to suit the larger grain vessels now using the port.
4.	More grain storage is needed
5.	More import-export storage needed
6.	Lengthening of the shipping season
7.	Competitive marine insurance rates for entire season
8.	Realistic railway rates comparable on a mileage basis with other lines
The next point is important:
9.	An all-weather highway from the prairies to Churchill.
10.	A concerted effort by all three provincial governments for more trade.
March 20, 1973

I think that outlines the reasons why we must put more federal money into that port. We must stop talking and start acting right now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister oi Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first wish to congratulate the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) on the very good presentation he has made tonight. I believe that what he said pertaining to the port of Churchill and the importance thereof is certainly true. I agree with him.
We have been most interested in the possible future development of the port of Churchill. The National Harbours Board will soon be submitting an economic study on the future of the port of Churchill to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). After reviewing this study, it is expected the government will be in a position around mid-April to state whether it is practical to take any action with respect to further port development in the area.

subtopic: BILINGUALISM-PILOT PROJECT TO TEACHING FRENCH IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL AREA-TEACHING OF ENGLISH IN FRENCH-SPEAKING SCHOOLS
BILINGUALISM-PILOT PROJECT TO TEACHING FRENCH IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL AREA-TEACHING OF ENGLISH IN FRENCH-SPEAKING SCHOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments about the announcement made last March 16 concerning the encouragement extended to the teaching of the second language in the schools of the Ottawa area, which provide $2 million for that purpose. As that assistance is so important, it certainly will be welcome in the area.
I would like to make some comments on that subject. First, I will say that if Canada is to remain or become bilingual, we must maintain in each province representatives of both official languages so that the two elements of bilingualism always be present in all provinces in Canada.
However, in the provinces where the French-speaking people are in minority, bilingualism will be in jeopardy if they can no longer develop fully in the French language and culture or if, because of difficulties or apathy, they decide to join the English-speaking majority.
All efforts made by the federal government will be of little use if we cannot maintain in all provinces a strong, lively, and dynamic French-speaking group which would lead the way and make a place for itself under the sun thanks to all sorts of provincial and public institutions designed to promote and encourage the French culture.
Without an official structure, without bilingualism or even French-speaking unilingualism in each Canadian province, the amounts provided by the federal government for promoting bilingualism could not stop the tide of English-speaking unilingualism.
The French-speaking people living outside Quebec are responsible for the success or the failure of bilingualism programs established by federal government in each Canadian province, and naturally I exclude the province of Quebec.
Those efforts towards the establishment of bilingualism, Francophones have made them since our country was founded, but under present circumstances, the fran-
Adjoumment Debate
cophone minority can no longer oppose single-handed the anglophone giant of unilingualism. They must be given specific and efficient help if they are to continue living and fulfilling themselves in French
The $300 million federal assistance program which is to run over a five-year period must first encourage teaching of the second language, which is French in mostly anglophone provinces and English in Quebec. Secondly, provinces are to be encouraged to maintain an educational system for minorities.
This is a very worthwhile program and if I had the figures-which unfortunately I have not-showing how this money has been spent by the provinces, I might feel easier to express my views.
According to my information, the province of Ontario would have received $14 million last year under this program. Five million dollars were to be spent for teaching the second language and $9 million for the francophone minorities.
On Friday last, the minister announced another grant of $2 million for the national capital area, which is an increase of 40 per cent. I rejoice at the federal government supporting the teaching of French to the English-speaking, especially since it subsidizes that teaching through an experimental program. But the French-speaking minorities have needs that would also benefit from similar programs, even if those minorities must do it by way of an experimental program.
May I mention certain education fields which are in need. For the Francophones who form a minority, there should be first of all a French school. And I recall that from 1955 to 1967 the federal government thought that the magic solution to the unemployment problem was partially in technical education, and justly so. Now, that same federal government did not hesitate to earmark millions of dollars in grants for building composite schools with technical departments.
If in 1973 the federal government feels bilingualism is important, should it not stimulate provinces by granting them subventions for the purpose of creating homogeneous French schools?
Federal grants for the teaching of the second language should be paid out with no ceilings, that is over and above the basic budget. Part of the federal government grants for bilingualism could remain in provincial treasuries for the preparation of manuals and teaching aids, the development of programs, etc. I have in mind audio-visual systems, for instance. Without a concentrated effort at provincial and federal levels, such teaching aids can never be obtained from regional school boards, which are often in a minority situation.
Mr. Speaker, I could discuss experimental programs within the framework of which relatively small grants could encourage francophone teachers to write French school manuals for our minorities. None of the provinces where there are now minorities are able to interest publishers in bringing out such manuals, because of the limited quantities involved.
Federalism could bring about a synthesis of the requirements of Ontario, Manitoba and New Brunswick for school manuals and audio-visual equipment. It is just a

March 20, 1973
Adjournment Debate
matter of regrouping the urgent needs of several minorities on a national basis. The federal government is carrying out experiments in the linguistic field and I agree with that, but I would agree even more if the government also launched a pilot program of assistance in the preparation and publication of school manuals and also in the production and distribution of French-language audio-visual teaching aids.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: BILINGUALISM-PILOT PROJECT TO TEACHING FRENCH IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL AREA-TEACHING OF ENGLISH IN FRENCH-SPEAKING SCHOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the foremost principles that the Secretary of State Department is proud to uphold and defend, and one to which I wholeheartedly subscribe, is the learning of a second language in provincial education.
Within the framework of the policy we have announced, which serves the aims of the bilingualism that we wish to foster and to spread, the Secretary of State Department announced a few days ago that it had signed an agreement with the government of Ontario, allowing for a supplementary budget for the teaching of French as a second language. If we wish bilingualism to win respect, it is only fitting, in my opinion, that the national capital should be a prime example. I believe my colleague, the member for Ottawa East (Mr. Gauthier), acknowledges that our English-Canadian friends do not have the opportunity to learn French as they would wish, and it is for the
Secretary of State to allocate supplementary funds for this purpose.
I should add that the Secretary of State Department has announced, through the minister, that it is prepared to further a project of similar proportions in Quebec, if the Quebec authorities should request this.
The question that my hon. friend has raised is, as he himself said, first and foremost a provincial one, since the Constitution lays down that the teaching of the first language, English in the case of Ontario, comes under provincial jurisdiction, and I am sure it is able to assume its responsibilities.
I should like to remind my hon. friend that this is a pilot project, which will no doubt lead to the development of new techniques that may help solve the problem he has raised.
I shall end my remarks by saying that the policy of the Secretary of State Department also provides for encouragement to minorities in the form of subsidies; my hon. friend is well aware that the Franco-Ontarions benefit from these advantages, and will continue to do so in future. It seems to me that, as a member of Parliament, my friend is eminently qualified to understand that the Secretary of State Department, through the minister, has a very open mind on the problems he has raised, and that we mean to pull together to try and solve them, at the same time enabling bilingualism to fulfil its true role throughout Canada.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10:26 p.m.

Wednesday. March 21, 1973
